📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Note, the release has been updated to include a quote from the National Security Division.

An eight-count superseding indictment was unsealed today charging Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, with terrorism-related offenses for their activities in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs), including their involvement in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States, and a September 2026 terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where American armed forces were stationed.

Recent findings suggest that “Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government,” remarked Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The defendants listed in the indictment allegedly supported two foreign terrorist organizations, and al-Saadi allegedly coordinated with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted terrorist plot. This Department of Justice will continue dismantling terrorist networks and protecting the American people from terrorist organizations.”.

“This eight-count indictment reveals the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the U.S., including one plot that was recently prevented at RAF Fairfield, a British Royal Air Force Base where American forces were stationed,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “According to the indictment, one of the subjects is behind bars awaiting trial yet he allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence. To date, the subjects have been allegedly involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (“IRGC”), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations. This FBI will use all our resources to detect and stop such terrorist attacks as we’ve done the last 21 months – with over 1,300 terrorists disrupted and nearly 7,000 Foreign Terrorist Organization related arrests, up 1,057%. All those who threaten our homeland will get the message – justice will find you.”.

According to recent reports, “Today marks a major disruption of an alleged global terrorism conspiracy,” noted Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “No matter where they are in the world, the National Security Division of the Department of Justice will pursue those who target American citizens and American interests. My thanks go out to the prosecutors and law enforcement partners for their work on this case.”.

“As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” stated U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of New York. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas. The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real. Our Office will not stop working to address and disrupt this threat, and to prosecute those responsible.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to the allegations contained in the superseding indictment and other court filings: Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and al-Hassani allegedly conspired to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the United States on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, both of which are FTOs. Most recently, in approximately September 2026, al-Hassani allegedly orchestrated a terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base (RAF Fairford) in Fairford, United Kingdom (the “RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot”), which at the time of the attempted attack, housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel.

Al-Hassani and Mohajeri, both of whom were in Iran at the time of the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot, allegedly relied on a network of contacts in the United Kingdom. Al-Saadi, who was imprisoned and awaiting trial on pending terrorism charges in the Southern District of New York, attempted to coordinate with al-Hassani and Mohajeri from jail by passing coded messages through third parties.

It has been revealed that al-Saadi, a longtime operative of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, was charged in May for working with and on behalf of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, as well as other FTOs, for his involvement in planning and promoting approximately 18 terrorist attacks in Europe; and for attempting to bomb a synagogue in New York. The picture below demonstrates al-Saadi in front of an array of machineguns in a conference room with a map of the United States on the wall next to a list of “legitimate targets” (redacted here) identifying former and current U.S. officials.

In a recent development, as alleged, among the individuals with whom al-Saadi worked to facilitate and carry out the European Terrorist Attacks were Mohajeri and al-Hassani. Mohajeri is an Iranian national and operative of the IRGC who coordinated with al-Saadi and al-Hassani to carry out those terrorist attacks with the IRGC’s backing. Al-Hassani, who is originally from Iraq, used his contacts and criminal associates to carry out terrorist attacks in the United Kingdom.

According to recent reports, the European Terrorist Attacks were carried out in the name of a purportedly latest terrorist group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which is a front for Kata’ib Hizballah and other FTOs. Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the United Kingdom, the most of any European country. The attacks involved arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual U.S.-British citizen.

Al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and Al-Hassani were allegedly personally involved in planning many of the European Terrorist Attacks, and al-Saadi and Mohajeri helped create and publish online propaganda videos of these attacks. For example, on or about April 6, Mohajeri and al-Hassani planned attacks while together in a room in Iraq with a map of London displayed on a computer screen. In a video of that meeting, al-Hassani told Mohajeri, “we need to get focused on London.”  An image of the video is below, with Mohajeri on the right and al-Hassani on the left. HAYI then claimed responsibility for six terrorist attacks that occurred in and around London starting approximately one week later.

On or about April 17, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri allegedly directed an individual to carry out one of the European Terrorist Attacks in real time. Specifically, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri, along with others, were in a room watching a FaceTime video with the individual who was carrying out the attack, which was projected onto a large screen against the background of the HAYI logo. Al-Hassani directed the perpetrators’ actions, including by instructing the individual on the other end of the call to execute the attack and directing that individual to take a lighter and “light one in your hand,” “light it,” and “throw the fourth one.” Al-Saadi recorded the attack in real time, while Mohajeri recorded al-Hassani and al-Saadi in the room as they directed the attack. A still image from Mohajeri’s recording, showing al-Saadi (circled in red) and al-Hassani (circled in green), as they directed and filmed the attack, is below.

Recent findings suggest that the next day, on or about April 18, al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London, with the HAYI logo projected on the background of al-Hassani’s screen. During the video call, al-Hassani directed the individual to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” The person on the video then lit an improvised explosive device and threw it at a building. An image from the video is shown below.

In March and April — overlapping with the time that al-Saadi was co-located in Iraq with Mohajeri and al-Hassani, planning the European Terrorist Attacks — al-Saadi allegedly attempted to coordinate and carry out terrorist attacks in the United States, including by targeting a synagogue in Manhattan.

On or about May 1, following the European Terrorist Attacks, al-Saadi was arrested abroad and subsequently transferred to the custody of the United States to face prosecution. Al-Saadi has been in federal custody since his arrival in the United States. For approximately four months following al-Saadi’s arrest, there were no additional attacks attributable to al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and al-Hassani.

In August, however, al-Hassani allegedly directed and paid associates in the United Kingdom to conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot. On Aug. 22, al-Hassani paid one individual (Individual-1) to perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford’s perimeter and al-Hassani subsequently received videos of the area surrounding the base. In later communications with al-Hassani, Individual-1 referred to him as “Ali.”.

In September, al-Hassani also tasked and paid several individuals to help him prepare for the plot, including by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel. At al-Hassani’s urging, those individuals commissioned custom decals that they affixed to the vans to create the appearance that they were used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business.

On Sept. 26, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base. That day, al-Hassani was in frequent communication with the van drivers, helping to coordinate their movements and directing them where to drive. At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route. Al-Hassani communicated with the drivers and occupants of the vans both before and after encountering the security checkpoint. In the early morning hours of Sept. 27, law enforcement authorities in the United Kingdom recovered three white vans to which the fuel delivery business logos were affixed and arrested the occupants.

In a recent development, while in prison in New York awaiting trial, al-Saadi has had phone calls with his immediate family members located in Iraq. As alleged, al-Saadi used those calls to pass coded messages to Mohajeri and al-Hassani in the days leading up to the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

Industry observers note that for example, in June and July, al-Saadi allegedly spoke with his mother and sister about Mohajeri. During those calls, they referred to Mohajeri by various aliases, including “Abbas, Abu Daniel” and “Sayyid Abbas.”  Al-Saadi also told his family members that he owed money to Mohajeri and directed them to pass along messages to Mohajeri about “work,” a term al-Saadi regularly used to describe terrorist activity, including on social media posts and in discussions with Mohajeri about partnering to conduct terrorist attacks. On one of those calls, al-Saadi also asked his sister, “What are they doing about all our old work?” and asked her whether it had been cancelled or just put on pause. Al-Saadi’s sister responded that “it isn’t cancelled.”.

On or about Sept. 24, al-Saadi once again spoke with his immediate family by phone. On the call, al-Saadi allegedly inquired about how al-Hassani, whom al-Saadi referred to as “Ali,” was doing. Al-Saadi’s family informed al-Saadi that “Ali” had been transferred to the “International Section.”  Al-Saadi then allegedly instructed his family to “give him [al-Hassani] money so we can do it.”  As described above, three days later, al-Hassani orchestrated the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

Al-Saadi, 32, is a citizen of Iraq and Iran. Mohajeri, 48, is a citizen of Iran. Al-Hassani, 35, is a citizen of Iraq. A chart containing the names, charges, and minimum and maximum penalties for the defendants is set forth below.

The Justice Department praised the outstanding investigative work of the FBI’s Fresh York Joint Terrorism Task Force, which consists of investigators and analysts from the FBI, the NYPD, and over 50 other federal, state, and local agencies, and the FBI Washington Field Office, Counterterrorism Division, as well as the assistance of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division, Counterterrorism Section, the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the NYPD, the New York State Police, and the Department of State.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jeffrey W. Coyle, Sarah L. Kushner, David J. Robles, and Chelsea L. Scism for the Southern District of Fresh York are prosecuting the case, with assistance from James Donnelly and Paul Casey of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today Justice Cody Hiland appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee. Senator Durbin quoted my blog post which called him unqualified, then totally botched the question. Durbin referred to me as a "conservative law professor," so he has the same problem as the New York Times. Alas, instead of asking why Hiland decided to air private conversations with law students, Durbin simply asked Hiland about temperament.

None of the other senators gave him even the slightest tough question. It's a shame, because he likely would have had trouble. This was one of the least polished circuit court nominees I've seen. Hell, Hiland made Todd Butler look like a pro. Is the process over? Well, I came across this posting from the retired senior editor of the Arkansas Times:.

Would news that a nominee for a federal judgeship twice failed the bar exam change the tenor of loud opinions on the exam rigging scandal?

For starters, it isn't entirely clear when Hiland graduated law school. Here is the line from his questionnaire. Is it 1998 or 1999? The stray 1999 is odd. Maybe he received the JD in 1998 but needed some more coursework to graduate?

According to the University of Arkansas Little Rock Bowen School of Law, Hiland graduated in 1998. Anyway, something is off here.

According to his Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire, he was admitted to the bar in 2002, but he does not indicate if he took the July or February administration.

I was able to find an article from the Arkansas Democrat Gazette from March 30, 2002 which indicates that Hiland passed the February 2002 bar exam. As a general rule, people take the February bar when they either (a) had some sort of conflict for the July bar or (b) failed the July bar.

Between 1997 and 2000, Hiland held various positions in the office of Governor Mike Huckabee. None required a JD. From 2000 to 2002, he worked as a Staff Attorney at the Arkansas Transitional Employment Board. It isn't clear to me how he could be a Staff Attorney before he was admitted to the bar. In 2002, after Hiland was admitted to the bar, he began as an associate at a law firm in Paris, Arkansas.

Usually, law school graduates immediately take the bar exam. Perhaps Hiland was too busy serving as an aide to the governor to do so right away. Maybe he took it for the first time in February 2002, either two or three years after graduating from law school.

If only President Trump asked Katie Zacharia when she passed the bar. It might be worth asking Hiland about how many bar exams he has taken in a Question for the Record.

    #8991. Israeli-American Emory Professor's Defamation Case Against CAIR Georgia and Emory Student Can Go Forward (in Part)

    Israeli-American Emory Professor's Defamation Case Against CAIR Georgia and Emory Student Can Go Forward (in Part)

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Some excerpts from the long opinion by Judge Thomas Thrash (N.D.
    • In a recent development, this action arises out of alleged defamatory statements that Defendant Umaymah Mohammad, a student at the Emory University School of Medicine, made about Plaintiff Joshua Winer, a physician and professor at Emory.
    • Nearly two months later, in March 2024, the Plaintiff published an op-ed piece in an Israeli news publication sharing his decision to travel to Israel to volunteer as a physician in the Israeli Defense Force ("IDF") following the October 7th Hamas attack on Israel.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Some excerpts from the long opinion by Judge Thomas Thrash (N.D. Ga.) yesterday in Winer v. Mohammad:.

    In a recent development, this action arises out of alleged defamatory statements that Defendant Umaymah Mohammad, a student at the Emory University School of Medicine, made about Plaintiff Joshua Winer, a physician and professor at Emory. Mohammad, who is Palestinian, sent an email to the entire School of Medicine student and faculty body on January 17, 2024, in which the Plaintiff alleges she "praised terrorism against Israel, expressed her hatred towards Israel and the United States, and stated that Israel, the United States, and Emory are perpetrating a genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.".

    Nearly two months later, in March 2024, the Plaintiff published an op-ed piece in an Israeli news publication sharing his decision to travel to Israel to volunteer as a physician in the Israeli Defense Force ("IDF") following the October 7th Hamas attack on Israel. The Plaintiff identifies as Jewish and maintains dual American and Israeli citizenship. He is a surgical oncologist at Emory Winship Cancer Institute, a professor in the Department of Surgery, Division of Surgical Oncology at the School of Medicine, and serves as the School of Medicine Surgical Clerkship Director.

    In April 2024, Mohammad participated in an interview for a news organization called Democracy Now!. In the interview, Mohammad was asked about the email she sent and was asked to explain the importance of the issue to her. As part of her response, Mohammad referenced Winer by stating that.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the professors of medicine we have at Emory recently went to serve as a volunteer medic in the Israeli Offense Force [sic] and recently came back. This man participated in aiding and abetting a genocide, in aiding and abetting the destruction of the healthcare system in Gaza and the murder of over 400 healthcare workers, and is now back at Emory so-called teaching medical students and residents how to take care of patients.

    It has been revealed that mohammad was ultimately suspended from the School of Medicine for one year based on her comments in the Democracy Now! interview. In November 2024, Mohammad participated in a podcast hosted by the International Union of Scientists in which she made similar statements about the Plaintiff. In January 2025, she made more statements about the Plaintiff's IDF service in the online publication Mondoweiss. In the Mondoweiss piece, Mohammad claimed that the Plaintiff "believe[d] in the legitimacy of apartheid, and that some human lives are not as important as others.".

    At the end of the piece, she provided a link to a social media post by Defendants National Students for Justice in Palestine ("NSJP") and Doctors Against Genocide ("DAG"), which ultimately led to a campaign on the website of Action Network that "contained additional false statements about Plaintiff and identified him by name." NSJP and DAG also published posts on Instagram regarding the Action Network campaign, which directly quoted Mohammad's Democracy Now! interview. These Defendants made a second Instagram post a few weeks later. The Plaintiff alleges that Defendant WESPAC is NSJP's fiscal sponsor and, therefore, "knowingly funded and facilitated NSJP's coordinated efforts to vilify Plaintiff and pressure Emory to discipline [him].".

    In February 2025, Defendant CAIR Georgia held a press conference on the subject of Mohammad's suspension, during which she made the following statement:.

    Recent findings suggest that [Emory] disciplined me for exposing Emory's complicity in the destruction of Gaza in an interview where I mentioned an unnamed physician who served in the military, actively engaged in the genocidal campaign against the Palestinian people, my people … I cannot learn from a physician who might have fired one of the 355 bullets that landed in 6 year old Hind Rajab's body. Or who might have helped make the decision to bomb one of the hospitals in Gaza. Or who might have celebrated the murder of our communities on the rubble still wet with Palestinian blood. A doctor who cannot see Palestinians as human beings will return to Atlanta to offer the same disposability to black and brown patients at home.

    CAIR Georgia, along with CAIR Foundation Inc. ("CAIR Foundation"), also issued a press release with a link to Mohammad's Democracy Now! interview and rebroadcasted this speech on its Instagram account on February 11, 2025. In this post, (the "IG Post"), CAIR Georgia also replied to comments by providing a link to a previously circulated email template and phone script that identified the Plaintiff by name and called for Emory to investigate him and/or terminate his employment.

    Industry observers note that mohammad's statements were later broadcasted and published by television stations and news outlets. Defendant Ibrahim Jouja was the President of Emory SJP when it shared NSJP and DAG's posts on the Emory SJP Instagram account, and also made or collaborated on similar posts sharing the Democracy Now! interview and identifying the Plaintiff "as a physician with military combat experience against Palestinians." Defendant Rupa Marya works with Mohammad as a cofounder of DAG and, the Plaintiff alleges, she has "frequently identified Plaintiff by name and used her social media platforms to spread harmful and reputationally damaging statements about him," including blaming him for the termination of a Palestinian professor at Emory School of Medicine and accusing him of participating in a genocide….

    Sources indicate that the court allowed plaintiff's federal claim for conspiracy to interfere with civil rights (42 U.S.C. § 1985) to go forward:.

    Section 1985(3) "created a cause of action against private individuals who, among other things, undertake conspiracies for the purpose of depriving, either directly or indirectly, any person or class of persons of the equal protection of the laws, or of equal privileges and immunities under the laws." "That § 1985(3) reaches private action does not, however, mean that it was intended to apply to all tortious, conspiratorial interferences with the rights of others." ….

    Sources indicate that the Plaintiff hinges [the remaining part of] his § 1985(3) claim on the alleged violations of his rights under … Title VI. The Eleventh Circuit does not appear to have addressed whether a violation of Title VI is enforceable against a private conspirator under § 1985(3), so for the reasons the Court expressed in its prior orders, the Court presumes that it is. To state a claim under § 1985(3), a plaintiff must establish that the defendant has.

    (1) conspired or gone in disguise on the highway or on the premises of another, (2) for the purpose of depriving, either directly or indirectly, any person or class of persons of the equal protection of the laws, or of equal privileges and immunities under the laws, (3) taken or caused an action to be taken in furtherance of the conspiracy's object, and (4) injured an individual's person or property or deprived her of exercising any right or privilege of a United States citizen.

    Title VI provides that no one shall "be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance" on the ground of his "race, color, or national origin." To state a claim under § 2000d, a plaintiff must only allege that the defendant receives federal funds, that it discriminated against the plaintiff on the basis of race, color, or national origin, and that it did so in the course of a federally funded program….

    Recent findings suggest that [Plaintiff asserts] a § 1985(3) claim based on a conspiracy to induce Emory to violate his Title VI rights. And for purposes of a motion to a dismiss, he has stated such a claim as to the CAIR Foundation theory. The Plaintiff alleges that CAIR Foundation receives federal funding, making § 2000d enforceable against it. More specifically, he alleges that CAIR Foundation received federal funding, that it conspired with the other defendants, including Mohammad and Jouja, to subject him to discrimination based on his race and national origin by posting the IG Posts at glitch, which he alleges were defamatory and filled with false accusations, and that this discrimination was carried out "in the administration of CAIR Foundation's program or activities receiving Federal financial assistance." The Plaintiff also identifies the specific actions he alleges the Defendants took in furtherance of the conspiracy, including the statements Mohammad made that Jouja is allegedly responsible for as president of Emory SJP. At this early stage, these allegations satisfy the elements of a § 1985(3) claim predicated on a Title VI violation.

    Whether this claim can withstand summary judgment is a question for another day. Accordingly, the Defendants' Motion to Dismiss is denied as to this argument.

    In the process, the court also held that plaintiff had adequately alleged the "protected class" element of § 1985(3), by alleging that he was targeted for his national origin:.

    It has been revealed that the Defendants next argue that the Plaintiff unfairly conflates anti-Zionism with antisemitism in order to "place an entire area of First Amendment-protected political, legal and ethical discussion off limits." … The Defendants essentially argue that because Zionism is (in their view) solely a political philosophy, the Plaintiff has actually alleged that their actions were not truly motivated by his Jewish identity but instead by their opposition to Zionism and serving in the IDF. But taking that view would require the Court to construe the Plaintiff's allegations narrowly and in their favor, which it cannot do at this stage.

    What the Plaintiff actually alleges, if construed in his favor—and what the Court must accept as true at this stage—is that his military service resulted from a "sense of duty to serve the Jewish homeland, which is integral to his racial identity as a Jew" ["racial" is here used in the historical sense that included what we would now call "ethnicity," consistent with the Court's caselaw on § 1985 and related statutes -EV] and that his association with Zionism is also "an integral part of Jewish identity for a very significant number of Jews." In essence, the Plaintiff alleges that his military service and association with Zionism are markers of his own personal Jewish identity, and that his Jewish heritage as an Israeli national is a protected class.

    Sources indicate that critical to this interpretation is the Plaintiff's allegations that his IDF service was tied to the duty he felt based on his nationality and the significance of Zionism in Jewish culture. These allegations suffice at this stage to demonstrate that a discriminatory animus based on a protected class—the Plaintiff's national origin—motivated the Defendants' actions, not mere political differences.

    In a recent development, and the court concluded that plaintiff had adequately alleged that defendants' speech fell within the First Amendment exception for defamation. It concluded that plaintiff had adequately alleged that he wasn't a limited purpose public figure, despite his op-ed. And the court concluded that plaintiff had adequately alleged that the statements about him contained false factual assertions:.

    Plaintiff asserts that parts of Mohammad's statement in the Democracy Now! interview are demonstrably false, including her statements that the Plaintiff "aid[ed and abett[ed] a genocide" and "aid[ed] and abett[ed] the destruction of the healthcare system in Gaza." Regardless of whether these statements express political opinion, the statements could reasonably "imply defamatory facts about the plaintiff that are capable of being proved false" when the facts are construed in the Plaintiff's favor[.] This is because Mohammad's statements—that the Plaintiff alleges Jouja is responsible for reposting as president of Emory SJP, along with supportive commentary—imply that the Plaintiff actively participated in combat operations during his service in the IDF, but the Plaintiff pled that he served.

    In a recent development, solely in his capacity as a physician, providing medical care to wounded soldiers. His involvement in combat was limited to situations in which his unit came under direct attack … Mohammad had no factual basis to claim that Plaintiff participated in or approved the bombing of hospitals in Gaza [or] celebrated the killing of Palestinians.

    The Court agrees with the Defendants' position that characterizing the Israel-Hamas war as a genocide is likely an inactionable opinion because it reflects a "subjective assessment, as to which reasonable minds could differ, [and which] cannot be proved false." But the statements at concern here go further and allege personal combat participation in the alleged genocide—a fact which the Plaintiff could prove at a later stage is false. At this stage, his allegations about his role are enough to satisfy the "false and defamatory statement" element of his defamation per se claim and the falsity element of his false light claim.

    The same is true of part of Mohammad's statement during the press conference, in which she stated that.

    Industry observers note that [h]aving a physician faculty member who participated in a military convicted of committing genocide against Palestinians makes me feel unsafe. It makes black and brown medical students feel unsafe. It makes black and brown and indigenous patients feel unsafe. I cannot learn from a physician who might have fired one of the 355 bullets that landed in 6 year old Hind Rajab's body. Or who might have helped make the decision to bomb one of the hospitals in Gaza … a doctor who cannot see Palestinians as human beings will return to Atlanta to offer the same disposability to black and brown patients at home.

    There are parts of the statement that express Mohammad's opinion, such as the part that the Plaintiff's military service makes her, and "black and brown medical students," feel unsafe. This is a subjective assessment that cannot be proved false, so this part of the statement is not actionable. But the part of the statement that suggests the Plaintiff might have been involved in combat decisions or actions and accuses him of not "see[ing] Palestinians as human beings" and offering "the same disposability to black and brown patients" at Emory certainly implies that the Plaintiff engaged in combat operations while serving in the IDF and that patients of certain races are therefore not safe in his care.

    The same is true of the statement in Emory SJP's March 28, 2025 collaborative IG Post that described the Plaintiff as "a physician with military combat experience against Palestinians." The Plaintiff has alleged counter-facts that, if accepted as true, prove these portions of the statements false, so the Plaintiff states a claim as to these portions of the press conference statement and the March 28 Emory SJP IG Post.

    Sources indicate that for these reasons, the Court will dismiss the portion of the Plaintiff's defamation and false light claims predicated on the opinion portions of the statements identified above. The Court will deny the Defendants' Motion to Dismiss as to the remainder of their First Amendment and opinion-based arguments….

    Sources indicate that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Data API Engineer to join our Data API Team and help improve the feature set, reliability and performance of our Data API, based on the PostgREST project.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

    Work on PostgREST’s PostgreSQL driver (based on Hasql) and remove bottlenecks and improve it’s performance.

    Work on PostgREST development of new features and bug fixes, aligned towards the goal of a multitenant Data API.

    Collaborate cross-functionally with other teams to debug and solve integration issues with the Supabase platform.

    Experience using the C language.

    Solid knowledge of SQL and plpgsql scripting in PostgreSQL.

    It has been revealed that strong track record of contributing to and engaging with open-source projects. Bonus points if you’ve maintained an open source project.

    Strong experience with providing technical support to consumers with varying levels of technical expertise.

    Experience with debugging applications under the Linux operating system.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    Industry observers note that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    According to recent reports, supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Sources indicate that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

Lewis, and J.R.R. Tolkien.The namesake of the lecture, famed scholar Russell Kirk (1918–1994), established the philosophical foundations of the modern conservative movement with his landmark books, The Conservative Mind (1953) and The Roots of American Order (1974). He was instrumental in the founding of National Review and Modern Age and was a distinguished fellow of The Heritage Foundation.Kirk’s political philosophy, summarized in his “six cannons of conservatism,” emphasized tradition and convention, transcendence and piety, political prudence, and ordered liberty. His application of those canons to contemporary challenges, through essays, lectures, and newspaper columns, was often provocative and controversial, but always noteworthy. Today, his works and legacy are being preserved and advanced by The Russell Kirk Center for Cultural Renewal.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • I thought I'd pass along this tribute, which I thought was moving and apt:.
    • Industry observers note that twenty years ago, I was elevated to chair the antitrust section of the State Bar of Arizona, and I needed a headliner to pack the room for my first event.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I thought I'd pass along this tribute, which I thought was moving and apt:.

    Dinner with Judge Richard Posner.

    Industry observers note that twenty years ago, I was elevated to chair the antitrust section of the State Bar of Arizona, and I needed a headliner to pack the room for my first event. Who in the world of antitrust could draw interest outside that world? The answer was obvious: the closest thing antitrust has to a rock star, Judge Richard Posner.

    According to recent reports, so I cold-emailed Judge Posner an invitation to address judges, lawyers and law students in Tempe. I doubted he would reply, but he did, rapidly. He would be happy to come—under one condition. I told him to name it.

    No antitrust law. Anything but antitrust law.

    It has been revealed that I agreed, of course. He could have lectured on gardening for all I cared.

    In a recent development, we all have our favorite jurists, past and present. Until last week, Judge Posner was my favorite living one. He died at 87. His writing is the reason I became an antitrust lawyer.

    Sources indicate that thirty years in the law, and I still turn to one trusted source when an concern is opaque or abstract. I run a quick Westlaw search for Judge Posner's take, and the fog lifts.

    Recent findings suggest that judge Posner wrote more than 3,300 judicial opinions, and he wrote them to be understood. He embodied what Judge Learned Hand preached nearly a century ago: "The language of law must not be foreign to the ears of those who are to obey it." Posner wrote for the people.

    Recent findings suggest that he turned abstract ideas into concrete images. Consider his advice to lawyers who ignored the law that cut against them: "The ostrich is a noble animal, but not a proper model for an appellate advocate." I'm not endorsing the tone, but the point slugs you in the jaw.

    Sources indicate that posner made hard things look easy, and he worked hard at it. He confessed to going through up to 20 drafts to give his opinions "a casual, colloquial, and spontaneous appearance." As he put it, "I admit to hypocrisy in working so hard to give the appearance of effortlessness!".

    In a recent development, judge Posner kept his promise and came to Arizona to speak on judicial independence, not antitrust. That night I hosted him for dinner at El Chorro, nestled at the base of Camelback and Mummy mountains.

    I was scared. What would I say to Richard Posner for two hours? Convinced I could not carry the conversation alone, I recruited reinforcements, including the Chief Justice of the Arizona Supreme Court and a neurosurgeon.

    I opened with a safe question. Had anyone seen any good movies lately?

    Posner went first. The last movie he had seen in a theater was Superman. In 1978. Of course. Of course that was the last movie he saw. He did not have time for those trifling pursuits.

    But then he leaned in. He and his wife had recently bought the first three seasons of 24 on DVD. Each episode, he marveled, captured one hour in a single day in the life of the protagonist, a man named Jack Bauer. A clock even appeared in the lower left-hand corner of the screen so viewers could watch the minutes tick by in real time. Posner narrated his favorite scenes as Bauer landed in one jam after another and always found a way out.

    I have told that story to my law clerks for years. Posner described 24 with the passion and precision he brought to his opinions.

    In a recent development, posner was an independent thinker who questioned what everyone else assumed, including his own views. He was a founder of the law and economics movement, building much of it with his longtime friend and collaborator, the economist William Landes.

    Recent findings suggest that posner moved antitrust from the boardroom to the checkout line. He asked whether the alleged anticompetitive conduct created efficiencies and raised or lowered prices for consumers. Courts had not always asked. The Chicago School has largely guided courts and regulators since the Reagan years.

    According to recent reports, I wrote one book. Posner wrote more than 50, ranging from Law and Literature to Reflections on Judging, all while carrying a full caseload. A 2000 study by Fred Shapiro ranked him the most cited legal scholar of the second half of the twentieth century.

    Posner's opinions will lift the fog for generations of advocates. A reporter once asked him how law schools could improve legal writing. He remarked he would have first-year students read Holmes, Learned Hand and Robert Jackson, then try to write with their clarity. Posner is on that list. Law schools should teach his writing.

    Western civilization is facing a crisis driven by mass immigration from the Muslim world. Across the Atlantic, the demographic consequences of Muslim immigration have begun to unravel the social fabric of Europe. America is following a similar course as its foreign-born population reaches historic levels. Coinciding with this trend, immigration from the Muslim world has increased dramatically in recent decades. After the Hart–Celler Act opened the United States to large-scale immigration from outside Europe in 1965, America’s Muslim diaspora has grown from roughly 100,000 in 1961 to more than 5.5 million today.[REF] Meanwhile, America’s Muslim population has more than doubled since the start of the Global War on Terrorism. If these patterns persist unchecked, they threaten to “change and corrupt the national spirit” of America.[REF]The growing prevalence of Islamic culture presents a host of practical problems for American society. Although Islamification is not yet a national threat on the scale seen in Europe, select urban centers and rural communities have started to become transformed by the influx of unassimilated Muslim immigrants. The West’s Muslim diaspora has demonstrated a striking aversion to assimilation. The case of Lewiston, Maine, where a wave of Somali immigrants has overwhelmed the city since the early 2000s, illustrates the problem. According to Lauren Gilbert, many of the Somali diaspora in Lewiston do not wish to assimilate into America’s “majority culture.” “Many Somali elders,” she reports from interviews, “view assimilation into the American mosaic as a threat to the very survival of the Somali people.” Accordingly, the Somali elders chose Lewiston, in part, “because they believed that they could raise their children and practice their religion in relative peace, free from unwanted outside influences.”[REF]Examples such as Lewiston’s Somali diaspora underscore how America’s embrace of multiculturalism has made it impossible to accommodate Islam without altering the character of the nation itself. As Gilbert acknowledges, “from a multiculturalist perspective, the desire not to assimilate and thus to lose one’s cultural and religious identity is a legitimate choice that the host society should respect and accommodate.”[REF] Many Muslim immigrants and their children reject the traditional “melting pot” settlement that integrated previous waves of immigrants into a unified American national identity.A 2026 op-ed in The Washington Post by Shadi Hamid, a senior fellow at Georgetown University, exemplifies this view. Hamid argues against the premise that “a minority community’s right to be in the United States depends on its willingness to converge with the cultural mainstream.”[REF] In Hamid’s view, “America was not founded on the assumption that its citizens would eventually come to agree on foundational questions.”This sentiment is widely shared by prominent Islamic organizations across America. The Council on American-Islamic Relations’ (CAIR’s) 2026 Civil Rights Report explicitly criticizes the old American tradition on immigration that sought to “preserve the ideal of U.S. homogeneity” and all attempts to restore the vision of America as united by a “single heritage.”[REF] To this end, the report asserts CAIR’s commitment to protecting Muslims’ “right to be different.” A 2009 article reposted by CAIR, which includes “assimilation” in a list of terms “not to use with Muslims,” is further indicative of this prevailing sentiment.[REF] In this same spirit, the Islamic Circle of North America declared in a statement issued ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11 that they “reject the premise that American belonging is contingent on loyalty tests or displays of patriotism.”[REF]Contrary to Hamid’s supposition, the Western tradition has long maintained that a republic depends, as Cicero would say, upon a fundamental agreement on justice and the common good. Mass immigration from civilizations with radically different political theologies and conceptions of justice, whose adherents refuse to adopt American cultural mores and the American tradition of ordered liberty, threatens the very existence of that tradition.The old tradition on immigration was rooted in the conviction that “America must be kept American.”[REF] That tradition recognized that too much immigration that is too disparate in culture, religion, and mores would change America’s regime of natural rights, self-government, and ordered liberty into something both foreign and undesirable. On this basis, the Founders would have viewed mass immigration from the Muslim world, and elsewhere, as a threat to both the country’s political and cultural heritage.The Naturalization Acts of the Early Republic, which largely prohibited naturalization of immigrants from outside the Western world, epitomized this consensus. This precedent was subsequently affirmed by the Reconstruction Congress and by several decades of judicial precedents from the early 20th century. Together, these various writings, debates, speeches, statutes, and court opinions form a consistent political tradition that endured for 175 years, beginning with the Naturalization Act of 1790 until the passage of Hart–Celler in 1965. Restoring this tradition offers the surest guide for navigating the challenges posed by mass immigration. What follows is a reconstruction of this tradition’s prevailing ethos.The Founders on Immigration and Republican CitizenshipThe Founding Fathers did not directly address the question of Muslim immigration or the compatibility of the Islamic faith with American society. The dilemmas of late modernity, in many respects, are unique in the history of the nation. As a result, modern Americans cannot simply look back to the Founding generation for a manual on how to solve the crisis of this age. Nevertheless, the Founders thought deeply about the fundamental principles pertaining to those questions—the nature of citizenship in a republic, the moral conditions of freedom, and the need to preserve a common national sentiment. These general principles provide a star and compass for navigating the challenges posed by mass immigration from both the Islamic world and elsewhere.Immigration raises vital questions for political life. A political community, Aristotle writes, “does not arise from any chance multitude” of individuals.[REF] The character of any given political regime depends on the character of its people. If that character changes, the very nature of the regime will change along with it. Aristotle thus warns that a “dissimilarity of stock” caused by an influx of foreigners facilitates regime change by introducing competing and often irreconcilable interests and notions of justice. The Founders likewise worried that indiscriminate immigration would threaten the stability of the republic by undermining national solidarity and transforming American society into “a heterogeneous, incoherent, distracted mass.”[REF]The Founders worried that indiscriminate immigration would threaten the stability of the republic by undermining national solidarity and transforming American society into ‘a heterogeneous, incoherent, distracted mass.’A country’s dominion over its borders is a core aspect of national sovereignty. The abrogation of the 13 colonies’ authority to promote or restrict immigration as they deemed fit was among the principal grievances against the British crown listed in the Declaration of Independence. The Founding generation established the Constitution to “secure the Blessings of Liberty to [themselves] and [their] Posterity.” For the benefit and preservation of those people—the original parties to the social compact and their heirs—Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution grants Congress plenary authority to establish a “uniform Rule of Naturalization,” that is, to dictate the terms on which the American people are willing to consent to the admission of foreigners.[REF]The Founders’ views on immigration flowed from their understanding of society as a social compact. “The body politic,” explains John Adams in the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780, “is formed by a voluntary association of individuals: It is a social compact, by which the whole people covenants with each citizen, and each citizen with the whole people, that all shall be governed by certain laws for the common good.”[REF] Through the ratification of the Constitution, the American people were bound together within a unified body politic by common consent. Accordingly, foreigners wishing to become citizens first had to receive the consent of the American people, who reserve the right to expand or restrict the criteria for new membership as they deem fit. As Gouverneur Morris observed during the Constitutional Convention, “every society from a great nation down to a club [has] the right of declaring the conditions on which new members should be admitted.”[REF]From the outset of America’s history, the Founders permitted deserving foreigners to join the social compact and enjoy the privileges and immunities of citizenship on an equal basis with native-born Americans. In this spirit, George Washington expressed his hope “that this land might become a safe & agreeable Asylum to the virtuous & persecuted part of mankind, to whatever nation they might belong.”[REF] The Founders’ liberality was not unqualified, however. Washington’s attitude conveys a degree of both openness and exclusivity. America would remain open to immigrants, but only to those “who are determined to be sober, industrious & virtuous members of Society.”[REF]For Washington, virtue encompasses both good moral character (“sober” and “industrious”) and the habits of good citizenship. As he explained to the Hebrew Congregation at Newport, America would extend the blessings of civil and religious liberty to whoever “should demean themselves as good citizens” (emphasis added) by giving to the government of the United States “on all occasions their effectual support.”[REF] Among the duties the Founders deemed essential for good citizenship is the rightly ordered love of country. Washington treats this civic obligation as equally binding on every member of the social compact, regardless of his national origin. “Citizens, by birth or choice, of a common country, that country has a right to concentrate your affections,” Washington wrote in his Farewell Address. “The name of American, which belongs to you in your national capacity, must always exalt the just pride of patriotism more than any appellation derived from local discriminations.”[REF]The Founders expected more from prospective citizens than a mere verbal affirmation of faith in the American creed. Immigrants were called upon to meaningfully integrate into America’s national heritage.In essence, the Founders believed that the preservation of the republic depends on the existence of a national identity shaped by what today is called culture, that is, a shared way of life defined by things loved in common. “The safety of a republic,” Hamilton observed, “depends essentially on the energy of a common National sentiment; on a uniformity of principles and habits; on the exemption of the citizens from foreign bias, and prejudice; and on that love of country which will almost invariably be found to be closely connected with birth, education and family.”[REF] (Emphasis added.)Naturally, the influx of foreigners threatens this civil harmony, since immigrants are “apt to bring with them attachments to the persons they have left behind; to the country of their nativity, and to its particular customs and manners.” Hamilton thus warns that the “unqualified admission of foreigners” would transform American society into “a heterogeneous compound,” “change and corrupt the national spirit,” “introduce foreign propensities,” and be akin to admitting “the Grecian Horse into the Citadel of our Liberty and Sovereignty.”Thomas Jefferson expressed similar concerns about the unqualified “importation of foreigners” in his Notes on the State of Virginia. “Suppose 20 millions of republican Americans,” he observes, “thrown all of a sudden into France, what would be the condition of that kingdom? If it would be more turbulent, less happy, less strong, we may believe that the addition of half a million of foreigners to our present numbers would produce a similar effect here.”[REF] Fearing this result, the Founders expected more from prospective citizens than a mere verbal affirmation of faith in the American creed. Immigrants were called upon to meaningfully integrate into America’s national heritage.The Founders had a clear understanding of what defined that heritage. “Every species of government has its specific principles,” Jefferson observes. “Ours perhaps are more peculiar than those of any other in the universe. It is a composition of the freest principles of the English constitution, with others derived from natural right and natural reason.”[REF] These two sources, creed and culture together, represent the core elements of America’s national heritage.Jefferson famously remarked that the Declaration did not aim at “originality of principle or sentiment,” but merely “was intended to be an expression of the American mind.”[REF] However, he could not boast that “all American whigs thought alike” if the American people did not first share a common way of life. Though the Declaration appeals to abstract, metaphysical truths, these were proclaimed by a people who shared a common political and cultural heritage.[REF] The We of the Declaration were those whose “forefathers, inhabitants of the island of Great-Britain, left their native land, to seek on these shores a residence for civil and religious freedom.”[REF] This cultural and political lineage serves as the foundation of America’s national heritage, the roux of the proverbial melting pot. As Thomas G. West observes, “it is unlikely that the American Revolution could have succeeded without something like the Anglo-American people with their distinctive ethnic character, religion, and legal heritage.”[REF] Reflecting this sentiment, John Jay boasts in The Federalist No. 2 how:Providence has been pleased to give this one connected country to one united people—a people descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion, attached to the same principles of government, very similar in their manners and customs, and who, by their joint counsels, arms, and efforts, fighting side by side throughout a long and bloody war, have nobly established general liberty and independence.[REF] (Emphasis added.)The Founders thus viewed naturalization as a process of both political and cultural assimilation. In a 1794 letter to Vice President John Adams, Washington expressed concern over the prospect of immigrants “retain[ing] the language, habits & principles (good or bad) which they bring with them.” He firmly maintained that if Americans were to remain “one people,” immigrants must become “assimilated to our customs, manners and laws.”[REF] As the younger Adams advised a German visitor, prospective citizens “must cast off the European skin, never to resume it. They must look forward to their posterity rather than backward to their ancestors; they must be sure that whatever their own feelings may be, those of their children will cling to the prejudices of this country.”[REF]The Founders wanted to ensure that immigrants would successfully assimilate into American society. Among their principal concerns was prospective citizens’ capacity for self-government. In general, they rejected the naive idea that, as stated by Theodore Sedgwick, “the subjects of all Governments, Despotic, Monarchical, and Aristocratical, are, as soon as they set foot on American ground, qualified to participate in administering the sovereignty of our country.”[REF] Beginning with the Naturalization Act of 1790 and culminating in the Naturalization Act of 1802, the Founders established clear standards for determining which foreigners were worthy of citizenship in a free republic.George Washington firmly maintained that if Americans were to remain ‘one people,’ immigrants must become ‘assimilated to our customs, manners and laws.The Founders’ various comments on immigration and the nature of republican citizenship illustrate four main criteria by which foreigners’ assimilability would be judged: they must be virtuous, affirm America’s republican creed, be loyal to their adopted home, and be culturally compatible. Each of these criteria was reflected in the provisions of the Naturalization Act of 1802. Addressing Washington’s concern that only those “who are determined to be sober, industrious & virtuous members of Society” should emigrate to America, naturalization was limited to individuals of “good moral character.” To ensure that immigrants were devoted republicans, immigrants seeking naturalization were required to matter an oath or affirmation proving their commitment “to the principles of the [C]onstitution of the United States” and relinquish any titles of nobility they may hold prior to naturalization.[REF] Meanwhile, loyalty to the United States was ensured by requiring petitioners to renounce all allegiances to foreign powers, indicating that the Founders would have opposed America’s current practice of permitting dual citizenship.[REF]In addition to these requirements, the Naturalization Act of 1802 dictated that prospective citizens undergo a probationary residency period of five years, declare their intent to seek naturalization three years prior to their application, and have been a resident of the state in which they filed their petition for at least one year. Naturalization petitions had to be approved by a court of “common law jurisdiction,” which in most cases were local county courts. In practice, courts often required two citizens to attest in a court of law to the applicant’s residency and that he was a devoted republican, possessed “good moral character,” and committed to the community’s “good order and happiness.”[REF]These requirements provided a system for validating prospective citizens’ ability to integrate into both American society broadly and the local community in which they intended to live. Furthermore, by involving local communities in the process of naturalization, the Naturalization Act directly operationalized the principle of consent. All parties—the immigrant, the local community, and the nation itself—in a sense had to approve the immigrant’s petition to join the social compact.The Founders described this process as an “apprenticeship” in self-government, whereby the “prejudices which the aliens had imbibed under the Government from whence they came might be effaced…before they were admitted to the rights of a citizen.”[REF] Simple affirmations of the American creed are not, Michael Leib of Pennsylvania observed, “magic,” which, “by hocus pocus, converted aliens suddenly into a fitness for citizenship.”[REF] The whole naturalization process thus facilitated the immigrant’s “transmutation” into an American. “It was this which gave the knowledge and feeling, and gave the opportunity, for the intercourse that amalgamated the aliens with us, and gave them a common interest. It was the surest standard by which to test the desire for citizenship; it was action, and not declaration; it was fact and not theory.”[REF] In other words, this process ensured, as Washington hoped, foreigners first had to intermix “with our people” and become “assimilated to our customs, manners and laws” to become citizens.[REF]In practice, these provisions provided little barrier to immigration during the Early Republic, but only because they were appropriately tailored to the peculiar circumstances of the era. Foreign immigration to the United States was negligible for a half-century following independence. From 1790 to 1820, the United States’ freeborn population (free whites and free blacks) increased from around 3.2 million to around 8.1 million.[REF] In his 1823 Annual Message, President James Monroe proudly remarked on how the nation’s population boom was “almost altogether native,” while “immigration from other countries has been inconsiderable.”[REF] Roughly 250,000 immigrants arrived on American shores in the four decades after independence, equating to just under 7,000 arrivals a year according to estimates.[REF] Fewer than 150,000 immigrants arrived between 1821 and 1830—roughly double the average from previous years but still a low percentage of the population.[REF]Meanwhile, almost all immigration during the Early Republic, and well into the late 1800s, came from the British Isles or Germany. As the U.S. Senate’s 1950 immigration report observes,the immigrants who arrived after the original colonists were of a racial stock [simply meaning Northwest Europeans] closely related to that of the original settlers. Their language was either the same or similar enough to make the acquisition of English comparatively easy, and their national traditions were harmonious with those already established in America.[REF]Consequently, the size and composition of the immigrant population eased the process of assimilation.Nor were immigrants entering a multicultural society. John Jay’s description of America as a people united by a common heritage is borne out in the demographics of the Early Republic’s citizen population. According to one estimate, at the time of the Constitution’s ratification, more than 90 percent of America’s citizen population were of British extraction in the 1790 census (83.5 percent English, 6.7 percent Scottish, and 1.6 percent Irish).[REF] Meanwhile, virtually the entire population in 1776 was Christian, with approximately 98 percent Protestant and the remainder Catholic.[REF] As such, the homogeneity of the citizen population in the Early Republic created a strong imperative for immigrants to “cast off [their] European skin” and integrate into our cultural heritage.These considerations, paired with the provisions of the Naturalization Act of 1802, ensured that immigration would not undermine the idea of America as “one people.” In this regard, the Founders’ views on immigration refute the notion that America was established as a nation of immigrants. The Founders’ immigration policy is best understood as a core element of American ethnogenesis, whereby “English, Scotch, Irish, French, Dutch, Germans, and Swedes” were “melted into a new race of men”—the American.[REF]The Founders’ views on immigration refute the notion that America was established as a nation of immigrants.In applying these principles to the issue of immigration from the Muslim world, the relevant questions are whether those populations have the virtues and habits necessary for self-government, are committed to the principles of republican government, will display loyalty to their new homeland, and are compatible with America’s cultural heritage. The following sections infer how the Founding Fathers would have answered those questions.The Founding Fathers on IslamThe Founding generation became acquainted with the Islamic world through trade, diplomacy, captivity, and war on the Barbary Coast. Generally speaking, the Founders came away from these interactions with the impression that Islam is incompatible with a free society.A noteworthy misconception is that the Founders’ commitment to religious liberty necessarily means they would have supported the integration of Islam into America’s body politic. Exemplifying this view, Denise Spellberg argues that “Jefferson and others defended Muslim rights for the sake of ‘imagined Muslims,’ the promotion of whose theoretical citizenship would prove the true universality of American rights.”[REF] As evidence for this claim, Spellberg points to the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, which, according to Jefferson, was intended to include “within the mantle of its protection, the Jew and the Gentile, the Christian and Mahometan, the Hindoo and infidel of every denomination.”[REF]Religious toleration and the freedom of conscience are undoubtedly American values but must be understood within the context of the country’s broader national heritage. The political culture of the Early Republic was not that of a secular society. Christianity served as the republic’s de facto national religion.[REF] As Joseph Story observes in his Commentaries, “the general, if not the universal, sentiment in America” at the time of the Constitution’s adoption was that any “attempt to level all religions, and to make it a matter of state policy to hold all in utter indifference, would have created universal disapprobation, if not universal indignation.”[REF] As such, “[t]he real object of the [First] amendment was, not to countenance, much less to advance Mahometanism [Islam] or Judaism, or infidelity, by prostrating Christianity; but to exclude all rivalry among Christian sects.”On its face, the 1796 Treaty of Tripoli seemingly contradicts the claim that the Early Republic rested on a Christian foundation and suggests that the Founders had no inherent opposition to the Islamic faith. It declares that “the government of the United States of America is not in any sense founded on the Christian Religion” and “has in itself no character of enmity against the laws, religion or tranquility of Musselmen [Muslims].”[REF] The treaty, however, should not be treated as either a reflection on the character of American society or a guiding principle for immigration policy. Its actual meaning is simply a rearticulation of the principle that every sovereign state is entitled under the law of nations to a “separate and equal station” among the powers of the Earth.[REF] The 1815 treaty with Algiers conveys the same sentiment in clearer language: “the Government of the United States of America has in itself no character of enmity against the laws, religion, or tranquility of any nation” (emphasis added), whether Christian or Muslim, free or despotic.[REF] The Founders’ respect for the right of sovereign Muslim states to govern themselves in accordance with their own customs and traditions suggests nothing about whether the subjects of those states would make good American citizens.That is not to suggest that the Founders categorically opposed granting citizenship to non-Christians. George Washington’s magnanimous “Letter to the Hebrew Congregation at Newport” proves otherwise. Indeed, the naturalization debates directly addressed the prospect of including a religious test and rejected the idea. Addressing the claim that the “good moral character” clause would serve such a means, Theodore Sedgwick answered for the majority that it “has no particular reference whatever to religion, or whether a man believes anything or nothing.”[REF] The Naturalization Act’s choice between offering a secular affirmation of one’s fidelity to the Constitution, as opposed to a religious oath, is further indicative of this prevailing sentiment.The freedom of religion is not unrestrained—the exercise of that right remains as subject to the constraints of ordered liberty as any other right.Even so, it equally does not follow from the Founders’ decision not to implement a religious test that a prospective citizen’s confession of faith was of no relevance to their fitness for self-government. An immigrant’s religious convictions did not give him a free pass to oppose the “principles of the [C]onstitution” or to act immorally, as determined by the community’s (primarily Christian) standards. The freedom of religion is not unrestrained—the exercise of that right remains as subject to the constraints of ordered liberty as any other right. No man “under colour of religion” may “disturb the good order, peace or safety of the State, or…infringe the laws of morality, or injure others, in their natural, civil, or religious rights,” states the Maryland Declaration of Rights of 1776.[REF]The standards which govern the application of this principle are even stricter in matters of immigration than when governing the conduct of citizens. To be sure, Jefferson’s sentiment that every American reserves the right to convert to Islam and freely practice his newfound faith holds true. It does not follow from this principle that the proliferation of every faith is healthy for the body politic. Nor does the right to religious liberty convey a right to join the social compact. The underlying principles of the First Amendment guarantee all American citizens the right to believe that monarchy is the best form of government, just as they guarantee the right to practice Islam. Despite this, the Founders wisely required immigrants to affirm their commitment to the principles of the Constitution as a necessary condition of naturalization. The freedom of association grants the American people the right to exclude whomever they may deem unfit for the mantle of citizenship. In exercising that right, the Founders recognized that the vast privileges and immunities afforded to American citizens imposed an even greater obligation to be discerning in who was permitted to join the social compact.In applying the “good moral character” clause, courts in the 19th century established that “whatever is forbidden by the law of the land ought to be considered, for the time being, immoral.”[REF] Any person who violated state law, or demonstrated a disposition to do so, would not be considered “well disposed to the good order and happiness” of the country and thus barred from citizenship. Early Americans generally viewed Islamic culture as antithetical to America’s distinctively Christian mores, particularly when it came to the family. John Quincy Adams’s criticism of Islam for “degrading the condition of the female sex” and for the faith’s “allowance of polygamy” is illustrative of this consensus.[REF] On these grounds, it is likely that some orthodox Muslims would not have met the Founders’ standard of “good moral character.”Supporting this conclusion, a federal circuit court reasoned in 1878 that the practice of polygamy disqualified an applicant from naturalization. The court further determined that any alien who insists that the civil law is wrong and maintains “that polygamy may be rightfully practiced…is not entitled to citizenship.”[REF] According to legal scholar Julian Lim, as America began to contend with its first wave of Muslim immigration from the Ottoman Empire in the early 20th century, Turkish nationals were subject to deportation for their doctrinal support of polygamy under the 1907 Immigration Act. This statute codified the courts’ earlier determination and largely carried forward the original intent of the Founders’ “good moral character” standard.[REF]Even granting Jefferson’s more pluralistic view of society, his writings on Islam indicate that he questioned the faith’s compatibility with America’s civic creed. Underlying Jefferson’s support of religious liberty was his belief that “reason and persuasion are the only practicable instruments” for the advancement of “true religion,” therefore, “to make way for these, free inquiry must be indulged” and promoted by society.[REF] In his private notes, Jefferson criticized “Mahometanism” for “stifling free enquiry” and for how “Mahomet [Mohammed] forbade free argument,” thus preventing any “reformation” of the faith.[REF] Accordingly, even if Jefferson abstractly supported the freedom of a hypothetical Muslim citizen to privately practice his religion, it is doubtful that he would be indifferent to, let alone welcome, the mass immigration of people he recognized as hostile to the principles of enlightened liberty.The Founders’ impression of Islam as a hostile force was solidified by their interactions with the Barbary States. The Algerians, writes an anonymous congressman from the First Congress,are taught as a maxim of their religion from their infancy, that those who do not profess the Mahometan [Islamic] faith are the natural enemies to their great Prophet, and his religion, and that it is their duty to destroy them—they therefore indiscriminately cruise against all Christian powers, and make prize of the persons of all Christians whom they take alive, and sell them into perpetual slavery, unless they will become good Musselmen, and swear to support the Mahometan faith.[REF]Jefferson and Adams reached a similar conclusion in 1786 following their meeting with the Tripolitan ambassador.[REF]The Founders saw in the Barbary States’ tyrannical impulse among the community of nations a reflection of the internal character of Islamic society. In 1817, Captain James Riley published his memoirs detailing his grueling experience under Arab slavery after shipwrecking on the shores of North Africa. He described the Islamic governments of the Maghreb as “in the strictest sense of the word, paternal” and akin to the “feudal system.”[REF] William Eaton, U.S. consul to Tunis and commander of the American expedition into Tripoli during the First Barbary War, had a similar assessment, expressing his sympathy for how the Tunisians are “abject slaves to the despotism of their government” and subjugated under the “worst of all tyrannies, the despotism of priestcraft.”[REF] Echoing these assessments, James Monroe later commented that the Middle East has always been dominated by “despotism[s] with great wealth and splendor at the head” and “slavery with ignorance, poverty, and wretchedness among the people.”[REF]Based on these considerations, Monroe argued that “Arabian[s]…Turk[s], [and] Persian[s],” among others, are not “capable of self-government.”[REF] His pessimism, however, was informed less by bigotry than by a reflection on history, which demonstrates “the effect which despotic Government has on the intelligence and manners of the people under it.”[REF] The disheartening and spectacular failure of the French Revolution confirmed for him this unfortunate observation. Monroe judged that if even “a great nation, distinguished for its improvement in civilization and in all the arts of civilized life” could not successfully balance liberty with public order, the prospects for self-government in the despotisms of Asia were even worse.[REF] Given that “those societies never had such government among them, or made an attempt to establish one, or showed any disposition to do so,” he concluded that “they are incapable of such [republican] government.”[REF]Monroe’s verdict that such societies lack the capacity for self-government is the creed-and-culture test in another form. Creed asks whether a people can affirm the principles of the Declaration and the Constitution. Culture asks whether their formed habits make that affirmation viable.The Founders worried that mass immigration from foreign despotisms could destabilize the republic.America’s recent ill-fated attempts to establish democracy in Iraq and Afghanistan largely vindicate the Founders’ concerns regarding “the dangers incident to an effort, by an old and populous community, which had been long ruled by despotism, to subvert that government and establish a free one.”[REF] Following the U.S.-led coalition’s invasion of Iraq in 2003, President George W. Bush optimistically predicted that “Iraqi democracy will succeed, and that success will send forth the news, from Damascus to Tehran, that freedom can be the future of every nation.” President Obama expressed a similar hopeful sentiment in his September 2012 address to the United Nations General Assembly, after the so-called Arab Spring, commenting that “freedom and self-determination are not unique to one culture. These are not simply American values or Western values, they are universal values.”[REF] Neither the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan nor the Arab Spring delivered on their lofty promise of a democratic Middle East. The Founding Fathers would have arguably concluded from these failures that their assessment of Islamic societies’ compatibility with self-government was well-founded, thus casting doubt on any such people’s fitness for citizenship.The Founders’ commitment to the principles of the Declaration made them equally critical of any society they deemed despotic and religiously intolerant. John Adams reproached Medieval Christendom as an “age of darkness” whereby the masses suffered under the despotism of “the canon and the feudal law”—the “two greatest systems of tyranny” to have sprung from Christianity.[REF] Following the French Revolution, Monroe leveled a similar criticism against the surviving Catholic monarchies of Europe, attacking them for depriving “man of his natural and civil rights” and raising “upon his religious faith…a long train of hierarchal establishments, which serve only to add to the power and the splendour of the court.”[REF]As such, the Founders worried that mass immigration from foreign despotisms could destabilize the republic. In 1803, the Louisiana Purchase raised for the first time the question of how to successfully integrate into the social compact, en masse, a foreign population lacking experience in self-government. Under the terms of the treaty, the primarily French-Creole population was to be “protected in the free enjoyment of their liberty, property and the Religion,” and in time, “incorporated in the Union” as citizens of the United States. However, the Founders believed that prudence warranted not immediately granting them all the privileges and immunities of citizenship.[REF]Following the acquisition of Louisiana, President Jefferson observed that “our new fellow citizens are as yet as incapable of self-government as children.”[REF] Congress accordingly organized the new Territory of Orleans in a manner reflecting the probationary period of the Naturalization Act. The French-Creole population would be ruled by a temporary colonial-style government administered by officials appointed by the President.
