Notably, Madison neither appeals to pluralism nor liberal toleration in justifying Catholics’ fitness for naturalization. He appeals instead to the principles of republican citizenship, observing that “there [is] nothing inconsistent with the purest Republicanism [in Catholicism].”[REF] In applying these standards to the prospect of Muslim immigration, the question then is whether the same could be mentioned about Islam. The aforementioned assessments of Islamic societies indicate that early Americans did not believe that a people kept as “abject slaves” to priest and sovereign possessed the independent character necessary for citizenship in a free republic.

    What the Founders criticized as the “despotism of priestcraft” can be attributed to Muslim societies’ adherence to Sharia law, which is predicated on the supremacy of Islamic law over secular authority. Indeed, it is for this very reason that Alexis de Tocqueville concludes that Islam is incompatible with free government. “Mohammed had not only religious doctrines descend from Heaven and placed in the Koran,” Tocqueville observes, “but political maxims, civil and criminal laws, and scientific theories…[t]hat alone, among a thousand other reasons, is enough to show that [Islam] cannot dominate for long in enlightened and democratic times.”[REF] There can be little civil or religious liberty in a regime where political authority is predicated on the word of the Koran and Hadiths, as interpreted by muftis and executed by the caliph.

    Islam embodies the manners and principles of a rival civilization that is largely incompatible with America’s national heritage.

    Sharia, as Tocqueville describes it, is not abandoned by a verbal profession of the American creed. It is a revealed civil and criminal code that rejects natural rights knowable by reason, popular sovereignty, equality before the law, and religious liberty. Moreover, it demands that its followers reject Washington’s commandment for citizens to “concentrate [their] affections” in the national community. Islam attaches its adherents to a transnational religious community, the Ummah, and divides their loyalty between two competing authorities, the Constitution and the Koran.

    Sources indicate that among the Founders’ greatest concerns about immigration was that people are apt to “entertain opinions on government congenial with those under which they have lived,” making it “extremely unlikely” that immigrants from a nation with opposing political principles “will bring with them that temperate love of liberty, so essential to real republicanism.”[REF] Even today, support for Sharia law remains remarkably high throughout the Muslim world—as well as among the ever-growing Muslim populations in Western Europe and the Anglosphere. Pew Research Center surveys published in 2013 found that 99 percent of Muslims in Afghanistan, 84 percent in Pakistan, 91 percent in Iraq, 89 percent in the Palestinian territories, and 74 percent in Egypt “favor making Islamic law the official law in their country.” Anyone who adheres to a theological code that is antithetical to republican government is not prepared to pledge fealty “to the principles of the Constitution of the United States.”[REF].

    By the Founders’ standards, adherence to Islam fails the test of republican citizenship on nearly every measure. It is not conducive to forming republican habits and virtues, it is at odds with the fundamental tenets of the American creed, and it demands allegiance to foreign theological codes and political authorities. In short, Islam embodies the manners and principles of a rival civilization that is largely incompatible with America’s national heritage.

    The Founders’ views on immigration from the Muslim world are not entirely hypothetical. In practice, they recognized that not all people could easily be integrated into American society. Those similar enough to America’s original settlers could gently be assimilated through residency requirements, oaths, and renunciations. Others were excluded. The Founders recognized that multiculturalism poses an existential threat to the stability of the regime. “In the composition of society,” Hamilton observes, “the harmony of the ingredients is all crucial, and whatever tends to a discordant intermixture must have an injurious tendency.”[REF] Consequently, the Naturalization Act categorically excluded from citizenship non-Westerners via the “free white person” clause. James Kent presumed that the clause excluded “the inhabitants of Africa” and doubted whether “the yellow or tawny races of Asiatics” were “white persons.”[REF] In effect, the Founding Fathers prohibited the naturalization of immigrants from the Muslim world.

    The “free white person” clause is understandably the most controversial provision of the Founders’ immigration policy, since it sounds to modern ears like a purely racial category. Its meaning, often misapprehended, and its underlying rationale, rarely investigated, offers valuable insight into the Founders’ approach to immigration. Notably, there is no documented debate in the congressional record surrounding the clause, suggesting that it was widely approved. Absent these records, the clause’s rationale must be inferred from the Founders’ broader political thought. In part, the clause can be attributed to the unresolved issues over slavery and the legal status of American Indians. More fundamentally, the clause exemplifies the Founders’ understanding of the moral conditions of freedom.

    Contemporary scholarship condemns this provision as part of “an anticanon of statutes [from American history] establishing and maintaining White supremacy.”[REF] Unable to look beyond the Naturalization Act’s anachronistic phrasing, critics fail to understand the Founders’ original intent or how their immigration policy squares with their broader political theory. These objections fail to appreciate the Founders’ principled statesmanship.

    The Founders presumed that individuals from outside the Western world were unlikely to exhibit republican virtue, affirm the American creed, or be effectively assimilated into the national heritage.

    Industry observers note that the Founders’ immigration policy was not, in essence, a narrow-minded racial doctrine. The naturalization restrictions were deliberate instruments for preserving a constitutional regime rooted in natural rights and republican self-government, made possible by a shared national heritage. The Founders recognized that a republic depends upon the character of its citizens. Far from bigotry, their approach reflected a clear-eyed assessment of what sustains ordered liberty.

    Under the provision’s original meaning, “white” did not have precisely the same biological connotation it eventually came to have in the antebellum South and progressive era. For example, Webster’s 1828 American Dictionary neither defined white as a racial category nor included the racial classification of Caucasian. Moreover, the common meaning of “race” in the Early Republic was more closely associated with what we would now call ethnicity.[REF] It is in precisely this register that Hector St. John de Crèvecœur referred to Americans as a “new race of men.”[REF].

    Accordingly, as Thomas West observes, the Founders’ various writings on immigration “show that they were thinking of civilization, not whiteness, when they reflected on the positive qualities that at least some European immigrants would bring with them to America.”[REF] If written in modern terminology, the early naturalization laws would likely substitute “free white person” with something like “Westerner” without losing its essential meaning.

    Recent findings suggest that the Founders’ use of race was, therefore, an imperfect proxy for a political and civilizational determination, a presumption about a prospective citizen’s habits, manners, and customs derived from their place of origin that spoke to their capacity for assimilation and self-government. In essence, the clause can be understood as a broader, more restrictive test of the same criteria screened for by the Naturalization Act’s other provisions. It reflects the Founders’ presumption that individuals from outside the Western world were unlikely to exhibit republican virtue, affirm the American creed, or be effectively assimilated into the national heritage.

    Though such views may offend modern sensibilities, the Founders’ prohibition of non-Westerners from naturalization is consistent with a proper understanding of the principles of the Declaration of Independence. Not all nations or cultures believe the principles of the Declaration to be true, and even fewer are equipped to put them into practice. As James Monroe illustrates, despite the fact all men are by nature equally free, because man is also “by nature a sociable being,” he is “in a great measure the creature of circumstances.”[REF] On this basis, Monroe argues that.

    no proposition according to my judgment, admits of a more satisfactory demonstration, than that in the formation of government, the condition of the society on which it is to operate is to be regarded; that the government which suits one state will not suit another, and that the most improved state of society is that which is best suited to the most free government, if it is not the only one that admits of it.[REF].

    Hamilton echoes this observation in a 1799 letter to the Marquis de Lafayette, noting that “a government must be fitted to a nation as much as a coat to the individual, and consequently that what may be good at Philadelphia may be bad at Paris and ridiculous at Petersburgh.”[REF].

    Recent findings suggest that monroe defined the ability of a given society to successfully implement the principles of the Declaration as “the capacity for self-government.”[REF] He viewed this standard as downstream from a nation’s “state of civilization,” which encompassed both a people’s understanding of the principles of liberty and their virtues relative to achieving that end. In his political treatise, Monroe observes that Europe is effectively the only quarter of the globe with a tradition of free government, the inference being that self-government must be the distinctive hallmark of Western civilization.[REF] He concluded from this premise that Arabs, Turks, Persians, and various other non-Europeans without an organic republican tradition lack the capacity for self-government.[REF] The “free white person” clause is an extension of this framework.

    This logic is most clearly illustrated through the Founders’ views on the legal status of American Indians. Although they were excluded from naturalization under the law, Jefferson expressed the Founders’ vision that eventually American Indians would be incorporated “with us as citizens of the US.”[REF] The major impediment to this project, in the Founders’ view, was a matter of “civilization,” not race. As Monroe explains, the “rude and unlettered state” of American Indian society “made them utterly incompetent to the discharge of the duties of a well organized, free, representative government.”[REF] Therefore, before they could become American citizens, they first needed to become “civilized”—that is to say, develop the habits and virtues necessary for republican citizenship and become assimilated into American society. Once this process was completed, they could join with their fellow Americans as “one people.”[REF].

    This broader, civilizational understanding of the clause was subsequently affirmed during the Reconstruction-era debates over the 1870 amendment to the Naturalization Act, which opened naturalization to “aliens of African nativity and to persons of African descent.”[REF] While expanding citizenship to black immigrants, Congress otherwise resoundingly voted to keep the free white person clause intact. The driving glitch was lawmakers’ concern that repealing the clause would grant citizenship to Chinese migrant workers who maintained their cultural and political allegiance to Beijing.

    Recent findings suggest that congress did not see this decision as inconsistent. Senator William Stewart (R–NV), one of the authors of the Fifteenth Amendment, expressed the majority’s reasoning as to how they could champion civil rights for blacks while simultaneously prohibiting naturalization from the rest of the non-Western world. Consistent with the Founders’ framework, Stewart explained that neither the spirit of the Fifteenth Amendment nor the Declaration of Independence required America to grant “political rights to all people throughout the globe.”[REF] Americans, he argued, “have a right to make our own laws; and it would be a crime in us to incorporate any people in the body-politic who are hostile to free institutions.”.

    According to recent reports, in Stewart’s estimation, American and European countries shared a common civilizational heritage, ensuring European immigrants would “assimilate rapidly” into American society. He contended that the same was largely true of blacks, who had grown culturally indistinguishable from America’s white population. “This was [blacks’] native land. He [the black American] was born here…. [H]e was an American and a Christian, as much as any of the rest of the people of the country.” By contrast, the nations of the Eastern Hemisphere “have another civilization at wars with ours,” one which does not “believe in republican institutions” and is inhabited by a people who “do not understand our society” or “value the privileges of citizenship.”[REF] Stewart concluded that such people were unfit for citizenship “until they changed their devotion to pagan despotism” and became either “republicanized or Christianized.”.

    Sources indicate that in this same spirit, the courts repeatedly determined throughout the naturalization cases of the 19th and 20th centuries that the Naturalization Act’s use of “white” reflected the common understanding of the Founding era—compatibility with Western civilization and not race. In the seminal 1878 case of In re Ah Yup, a California federal court excluded Chinese immigrants from citizenship, defining “white” according to its “well settled meaning in common popular speech” as encompassing Europeans and parts of Western Asia. To support its conclusion, the court drew on the congressional debates from 1870, citing Senator Oliver Morton’s concern that mass immigration from “another civilization” would have a corrosive effect on American society.[REF].

    In 1921, a lower court in Terrace v. Thompson, the precursor to the Supreme Court’s decision on the constitutionality of alien land laws, captured the essence of the Founders’ original intent. In his opinion, District Judge Edward Cushman opined on the dangers of multiculturalism, remarking that the courts had a solemn duty “to hold impregnable the barrier erected by Congress [via the Naturalization Act] to preserve, in its purity, our own type of civilization.” It was precisely for this reason, he concluded, that immigrants from outside the West were precluded from citizenship. The basis of this objection was not.

    due to color, as color, but only to color as an evidence of a type of civilization which it characterizes. The yellow or brown racial color is the hallmark of Oriental despotisms, or was at the time the original naturalization law was enacted. It was deemed that the subjects of these despotisms, with their fixed and ingrained pride in the type of their civilization, which works for its welfare by subordinating the individual to the personal authority of the sovereign, as the embodiment of the state, were not fitted and suited to make for the success of a republican form of Government. Hence they were denied citizenship.[REF].

    The Supreme Court subsequently reinforced this civilizational interpretation of the statute in two unanimous decisions. In Ozawa v. United States (1922), Justice George Sutherland held that Japanese immigrants were ineligible because they were “clearly of a race which is not Caucasian” in the popular understanding.[REF] In United States v. Bhagat Singh Thind (1923), Justice Sutherland determined that Indians were ineligible for citizenship, even if they were a “high-caste Hindu” who could be scientifically classified as “Caucasian.”[REF] Whatever the merits of this particular ruling, it hinged on culture and civilization, not race.

    The federal government’s brief in Thind reiterates the common theme that the Founding Fathers only intended to grant citizenship “for those whom they knew and regarded as worthy to share it with them—men of their own type—men in a general way living under the same social conditions, sharing or wishing to share the same political institutions and capable of entering into the life of this country in a spirit of sympathy and cooperation.”[REF] As such, the federal government argued that immigrants from the Indian subcontinent were precluded from citizenship because “at the time the first naturalization law was passed the Hindus were regarded as a people wholly alien to Western civilization and utterly incapable of assimilation to Western habits and customs, mode of life, political and social institutions.” The federal government thus concluded that “a free white person” according to the standard of “which the Congress has now adhered for a hundred and thirty years, denominates what is historically known as the men of the Western civilization.” It is this civilization “which our fathers knew and from which they were willing to recruit the citizenship of the Republic.”[REF].

    The Supreme Court agreed. Writing for a unanimous Court, Justice Sutherland declared that the statute used the term “white persons” in their “common speech” meaning as a stand-in for those who could “quickly merge into the mass of our population.” As he explained,.

    In a recent development, the immigration of that day was almost exclusively from the British Isles and Northwestern Europe, whence they and their forbears had come. When they extended the privilege of American citizenship to “any alien being a free white person,” it was these immigrants—bone of their bone and flesh of their flesh—and their kind whom they must have had affirmatively in mind.[REF].

    The bar was “assimilation.” European children “los[t] the distinctive hallmarks of their European origin,” while others did not.

    The old American political traditions’ keen sense of man’s social nature, and of what is now called culture, cannot and should not be dismissed as residual racism. Although a subset of lower federal court decisions during the early 20th century embraced the discredited theories of race science, they do not represent the overarching legal and intellectual consensus of the tradition. The prevailing theme throughout the major precedents on naturalization was the explicit rejection of any implication of racial superiority. Justice Sutherland stressed in Ozawa that “there is not implied—either in the [Naturalization Act] or in our interpretation of it—any suggestion of…racial inferiority.”[REF] In Thind, Justice Sutherland further clarified that the Court’s longstanding use of racial terminology, that is, “Caucasian,” was only because the term became colloquially synonymous with white, and was not an attempt to replace the Founders’ “common speech” terminology of the Naturalization Act with the “science of ethnology.”[REF] He also again emphasized that the free white person clause’s categorical restrictions were in no way premised on any idea of “racial superiority or inferiority.”[REF].

    Industry observers note that in applying the principles of this tradition to the modern immigration crisis, one can acknowledge that the Founders may very well have been overbroad in their determination of who is unassimilable. After all, the number of nations that now have experience with popular government has expanded considerably since 1776. Such qualifications, however, do not negate the validity of the underlying principle itself, which cautions against attempting to integrate people from civilizations whose social and political culture is utterly antithetical to the American way of life.

    The Founding generation was never tasked with applying the provisions of the Naturalization Act directly to the question of immigration from the Muslim world. When the matter finally arose during the 20th century, however, the enduring legacy of their principles resulted in widespread judicial skepticism over Muslim immigrants’ assimilability.[REF] Only when the old American political tradition was abandoned following World War II did courts determine otherwise.

    Sources indicate that prior to the Supreme Court’s decisions in Ozawa and Thind, the earliest precedents concerning immigrants from the Middle East involved Christians, namely Maronites and Armenians. These cases initially produced a circuit split, but a consensus eventually arose granting eligibility. Courts often cited Christianity and historical ties to Europe as evidence of civilizational compatibility for Syrians and Armenians. By contrast, Arab Muslims were presumably excluded from naturalization under the law. Because these cases were decided prior to Thind, some of the precedents over-relied on the discredited science of ethnology, often using an applicant’s Christianity as evidence of their “whiteness.”[REF] Of course, such reasoning makes little sense if “white” is defined biologically, but it is coherent if “white” is understood as a stand-in for Western.

    Sources indicate that in the 1909 case In re Halladjian, the federal courts came close to fully capturing the Founders’ original meaning. The government argued that Armenians were ineligible on the grounds that “white” meant European, not in the sense that the European-born child of a Syrian migrant may be considered today, but in that an individual culture embodies “the prevailing ideals, standards, and aspirations of the people of Europe.”[REF] In turn, Circuit Judge Francis Cabot Lowell’s opinion rejected the government’s conclusion by taking its appeal to a civilizational standard to its logical conclusion. Judge Lowell noted that though Armenians are not European, “the outlook of their civilization has been toward Europe,” as evidenced by their Christian faith and long-standing historical alliance with the nations of Europe against “both Saracens and Turks.” Therefore, Armenians were eligible for naturalization under the law because their cultural heritage ensured that they easily “become westernized and readily adaptable to European [Western] standards.”.

    This framework was applied directly to the question of Muslim immigration in In re Ahmed Hassan (1942). Consistent with earlier precedents, Judge Arthur Tuttle recognized that the qualifications for naturalization should not be “how the group in question would be classified by ethnologists who have made a study of racial origins, but, rather, what groups of peoples then living in 1790 with characteristics then existing were intended by Congress to be classified as ‘white persons.’”[REF] He reasoned that “it is well known that [Arabs] are a part of the Mohammedan world and that a wide gulf separates their culture from that of the predominately Christian peoples of Europe. [Therefore,] it cannot be expected that as a class they would readily intermarry with our population and be assimilated into our civilization.” Arab Muslims were thus deemed ineligible for citizenship under the law for the sake of preserving America’s cultural and political heritage.

    Sources indicate that precisely how and why the courts abandoned the Founders’ approach to immigration is revealing. Support for Muslim immigration began with the rise of a upcoming liberal consensus under the Roosevelt Administration and the shift towards globalism during World War II. In 1943, Roosevelt’s Department of Justice released an official position statement rebutting the conclusion of Judge Tuttle in Ahmed Hassan.[REF] The following year, in Ex parte Mohriez (1944), Judge Charles E. Wyzanski broke with 154 years of legal tradition and declared Muslim Arabs eligible for naturalization as “white persons” in line with the Administration’s guidance.

    Sources indicate that the conclusions of both the opinion and guidance rested in part on the Muslim world’s supposed compatibility with Western civilization. More fundamentally, however, Judge Wyzanski appealed to liberal internationalism and America’s role as a world power over the Founders’ republican framework. He argued that rigid exclusion was both antithetical to the “American creed” and “repugnant to our vital interests as a world power.” The purpose of America’s immigration policy was no longer to maintain a common national sentiment, but to serve as an instrument of soft power, whereby the government could promote “friendlier relations” with the non-Western world by integrating foreign cultures into American society.[REF].

    Echoing this view, President Harry Truman argued in his failed veto of the 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act that “our immigration policy is equally, if not more key to the conduct of our foreign relations and to our responsibilities of moral leadership in the struggle for world peace.”[REF] Truman’s message marked the beginning of the transition that would eventually culminate in the 1965 Hart–Celler Act. As Representative Jacob Gilbert (D–NY) observed, Hart–Celler was a “reaffirmation…of our enthusiasm for setting democratic standards for the rest of the world, [and] of our willingness to lead a global community of peoples toward universal recognition of human dignity.”[REF].

    Industry observers note that in many respects, Ahmed Hassan marked the culmination of a consistent legal framework originating in Ah Yup and refined over the decades by Halladjian, Terrace, Ozawa, and Thind. Together, these cases constitute a formidable body of precedent that faithfully applied the provisions of the Naturalization Act in accordance with the Founders’ original meaning. (See the appendix for a list of these cases.) In each of these cases, the Naturalization Act was interpreted not as a narrow biological test, but as a civilizational standard whose purpose was to preserve America’s republican character. America would remain open to immigration from across the West, while prohibiting naturalization from “hostile” cultures. In the words of Justice Sutherland, this principle deserved to be respected as “a rule in force from the beginning of the government, a part of our history as well as our law, welded into the structure of our national polity by a century of legislative and administrative acts and judicial decisions.”[REF].

    It has been revealed that after World War II, the newly established liberal consensus began to displace the long-standing American tradition on immigration. The year 1965 was a watershed moment in the establishment of new modes and orders. Today’s crisis is the result of that new system’s failure. What remains is a task of rediscovery, restoration, and adaptation. If America is to preserve its national heritage, it should recover the old American tradition on immigration rooted in the Founders’ theory of republican citizenship.

    Critics of that tradition reflexively label any concern about civilizational compatibility as xenophobic, bigoted, or racist. According to their logic, to question mass immigration because of its threat to republican government is to forsake America’s commitment to the principles of the Declaration.[REF] In truth, such critics really challenge the Founders’ ends as well as their means. Their commitment to multiculturalism demands that America accommodate and even celebrate foreign ways of life, however many foreigners arrive and whatever their political theology, family structure, or attitudes toward self-government. The critics’ open-ended cosmopolitanism aligns less with the principles of the Founding than with a deracinated globalism detached from the American people’s traditional way of life.

    The central question for statesmanship today is not whether immigration restrictions are “politically correct,” but what must be done to preserve the moral and political character of America. Though the old tradition may be controversial by modern standards, it was much more just and sensible than the current status quo of mass immigration. The Founders’ system of selective immigration committed no violence against those it excluded. Non-Americans have no inherent right to the privileges and immunities of American citizenship. Admission into the social compact rests wholly on the affirmative consent of the American people, who alone determine whether it serves their best interest.

    The central question for statesmanship today is not whether immigration restrictions are ‘politically correct,’ but what must be done to preserve the moral and political character of America.

    Recent findings suggest that statesmen today cannot simply reinstate the language or the policies of the Founding era, but they can recover and apply their underlying principles to modern realities. The Founders understood that America’s immigration policy must adapt as prudence demands. “In the infancy of the country,” Hamilton wrote in 1802, “with a boundless waste to people, it was politic to give a facility to naturalization; but our situation is now changed.”[REF] How much greater is the force of this observation after the closing of the frontier and decades of mass immigration that have severely tested the limits of assimilation?

    In a recent development, retrieving the long-standing vision of the American Founding will require an immigration system that once again recognizes that the will and faculty to be “assimilated into our civilization” is a non-negotiable prerequisite for good citizenship. “Hyphenated Americans,” who value the cultural heritage of their foreign ancestors over their status as American citizens, fail the test of assimilation. Immigrants may sometimes boost gross domestic product, but if they are unwilling to fully integrate into the American way of life, they do not belong in American society. Calvin Coolidge captured the essence of this ethos in his “First Annual Message”:.

    Industry observers note that american institutions rest solely on good citizenship. They were created by people who had a background of self-government. Latest arrivals should be limited to our capacity to absorb them into the ranks of good citizenship. America must be kept American. For this purpose, it is necessary to continue a policy of restricted immigration.[REF].

    Sources indicate that islamic culture poses distinctive challenges to the task of assimilation. However, Americans need not, and should not, resort to the crude and arbitrary racial categories of the past. Though the original meaning of the “free white person” clause is misunderstood, its structure and tone are still dissonant to contemporary ears. Even in the clause’s heyday, it was recognized as a blunt instrument with serious limitations, as illustrated by the Ozawa decision. Takao Ozawa was a resident of the United States for two decades prior to his application, college educated, a man of good moral character who attended an American Christian church, “maintained the use of the English language in his home,” and “educated his children in American schools.” By the Supreme Court’s own admission, “he was well qualified by character and education for citizenship.” He was still denied the privilege under a strict interpretation of the law.[REF].

    Whether someone can be scientifically or colloquially classified as “white” is not a reliable measure of one’s capacity for self-government. What matters for immigration is whether someone can be “assimilated to our customs, manners and laws.” Many immigrants from the Muslim world do not pass that test. New immigration reforms might achieve the Founders’ goal of ensuring that prospective citizens possess the capacity for self-government and preserve the nation’s traditional heritage, while also recognizing that the sphere of assimilable cultures could be larger than the Founders anticipated.

    Sources indicate that A cornerstone of the Founders’ immigration policy was that prospective citizens be persons of “good moral character,” a requirement that still remains in statute.[REF] This standard could be expanded to exclude anyone who practices or otherwise believes in the legitimacy of certain cultural practices or tenets of Islamic law that are antithetical to the moral sense of the American people and the principles of the natural law. This includes polygamy, first-cousin and child marriage, marital assault, female genital mutilation, honor killings, and the tenet that apostates be condemned to death.

    To be clear, such prohibitions would not amount to a religious test, as the glitch at hand is not whether someone affirms the Shahada. The proposed standard is predicated on the recognition that an individual’s “moral character” is inseparable from their moral convictions, regardless of their reason for believing so. This standard is consistent with the American tradition of ordered liberty, which has never permitted an individual “under colour of religion” to “infringe the laws of morality.”[REF].

    According to recent reports, A worthy model for broader reform is the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, otherwise known as the McCarran–Walter Act. The U.S. Senate’s 1950 report on immigration, which laid the groundwork for McCarran–Walter, recognized that.

    in times of peace, as in times of war, it has been clearly demonstrated that the protection of the public safety requires the exclusion from the United States of those aliens who bring with them their alien ideologies which are subversive to the national security and contrary to our constitutional form of government.[REF].

    The act thus implemented additional safeguards to ensure that immigrants were attached to the principles of the Constitution by prohibiting both the admission and naturalization of individuals “who advocate the economic, international, and governmental doctrines of world communism or the establishment in the United States of a totalitarian dictatorship.”[REF].

    America should choose to reaffirm the Founders’ theory of republican citizenship over the post-1965 settlement that treats America as a multicultural economic zone.

    Current immigration law maintains a weakened version of this prohibition against the admission of individuals “who favor totalitarian forms of government.”[REF] These prohibitions should be strengthened to prohibit the immigration of anyone fostering alien, totalitarian ideologies, and it should expand the definition to include anyone who advocates or affirms a belief in theocracy or the implementation of Sharia law as a formal, state-governed legal system or is otherwise affiliated with an organization that does the same.

    Industry observers note that the McCarran–Walter Act also recognized the need to preserve the nation’s traditional heritage. The act repealed the “free white person” clause after 162 years but adapted its underlying principles to the modern world by maintaining the use of national-origin preferences to ensure the preservation of America’s national heritage. The U.S. Senate report explained that this system was not premised on “any theory of Nordic superiority,” but was rather “a rational and logical method of numerically restricting immigration in such a manner as to best preserve the sociological and cultural balance in the population of the United States.”[REF] Conservatives should regain the conviction, held by previous generations, “that the peoples who made the greatest contribution to the development of this country [are] fully justified in determining that the country [is] no longer a field for future colonization.”.

    It has been revealed that to confront the current crisis, America should choose to reaffirm the Founders’ theory of republican citizenship over the post-1965 settlement that treats America as a multicultural economic zone. The choice is between an immigration policy whose purpose is to preserve America’s civilizational heritage and a policy whose purpose is regime change. The alternative promises the very consequences the Founders feared: a different country, no longer anchored in the social compact of a particular people united by a common heritage. Justice demands that Americans choose preservation as is their right and duty to future generations.

    #8982. "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Broad Evidence, and Silently Consistent Precedents"

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2278 w)

    "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Broad Evidence, and Silently Consistent Precedents"

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I thought I'd serialize my fresh Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the first Part:.
    • It has been revealed that in certain areas, First Amendment precedent turns out to be quite consistent with original meaning—even though the Court hasn't squarely discussed historical evidence in any detail.
    • It has been revealed that in some situations, this observation may not be accurate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I thought I'd serialize my fresh Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the first Part:.

    It has been revealed that in certain areas, First Amendment precedent turns out to be quite consistent with original meaning—even though the Court hasn't squarely discussed historical evidence in any detail. This might be a fortunate accident, or perhaps a random coincidence in the policy judgments of the modern Court and the Framing generation. But I expect that some at least stems from a phenomenon that Justice Scalia discussed in McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission (1995): "Principles of liberty fundamental enough to have been embodied within constitutional guarantees are not readily erased from the Nation's consciousness. A governmental practice that has become general throughout the United States, and particularly one that has the validation of long, accepted usage, bears a strong presumption of constitutionality.".

    It has been revealed that in some situations, this observation may not be accurate. But in others, there really does appear to be a longstanding constitutional understanding that has become so much part of the law that a court that simply follows doctrine will incorporate original meaning. Let me offer three examples.

    A. "The Liberty of the Press Is Not Confined to Newspapers and Periodicals".

    Industry observers note that the Supreme Court has generally held that the First Amendment equally protects all who speak to the public, whether they are professional media (e.g., newspaper publishers or reporters) or nonprofessionals (e.g., leafletters). In this respect, it has treated "the freedom … of the press" as protecting the press as technology—the use of the printing press and its technological heirs—rather than the press as industry, in the sense of people whose daily job is writing for the public.

    Now the original articulation of this position in the Supreme Court came in Lovell v. City of Griffin (1938), with little historical analysis:.

    Sources indicate that the liberty of the press is not confined to newspapers and periodicals. It necessarily embraces pamphlets and leaflets. These indeed have been historic weapons in the defense of liberty, as the pamphlets of Thomas Paine and others in our own history abundantly attest. The press in its historic connotation comprehends every sort of publication which affords a vehicle of information and opinion.

    And this is so even though the Court had shown an interest in Framing-era history. Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson (1931) discussed that history in striking down an injunction against the operation of a "scandalous" newspaper. Grosjean v. American Press Co. (1936) discussed history in considerably more detail in holding unconstitutional a selective tax on certain newspapers.

    More recently, Justice Scalia's concurrence in Citizens United v. FEC (2010) offered a bit more historical analysis:.

    Recent findings suggest that the dissent … interpret[s] the Freedom of the Press Clause to refer to the institutional press (thus demonstrating, according to the dissent, that the Founders "did draw distinctions—explicit distinctions—between types of 'speakers,' or speech outlets or forms"). It is passing strange to interpret the phrase "the freedom of speech, or of the press" to mean, not everyone's right to speak or publish, but rather everyone's right to speak or the institutional press's right to publish. No one thought that is what it meant. Patriot Noah Webster's 1828 dictionary contains, under the word "press," the following entry:.

    "Liberty of the press, in civil policy, is the free right of publishing books, pamphlets or papers without previous restraint; or the unrestrained right which every citizen enjoys of publishing his thoughts and opinions, subject only to punishment for publishing what is pernicious to morals or to the peace of the state.".

    As the Court's opinion describes, our jurisprudence agrees with Noah Webster and contradicts the dissent.

    "The liberty of the press is not confined to newspapers and periodicals. It necessarily embraces pamphlets and leaflets…. The press in its historical connotation comprehends every sort of publication which affords a vehicle of information and opinion.".

    But this is still predominantly a precedential analysis, with one textual argument and one early republican source.

    At the same time, the foundational case in the Court—Lovell—followed 150 years of established practice, to the point that the Court might not have seen the need to do more than just nod to "[t]he press in its historic connotation.".

    As I've laid out elsewhere, Framing-era legal sources, such as cases, treatises, and constitutional provisions, articulated the freedom of the press as extending to everyone, not just to professional newspaper publishers. {See generally Eugene Volokh, Freedom for the Press as an Industry, or for the Press as a Technology? From the Framing to Today, 160 U. Pa. L. Rev. 459 (2012) [hereinafter Volokh, Freedom for the Press]; Eugene Volokh, The Press Clause: Crucial, Remembered, and Equally Shared, 5 J. Free Speech L. 659 (2025).} Then, starting in the 1820s, courts began to expressly hold that newspaper printers' and editors' rights were equal to everyone else's. In the following decades, that was repeated in case after case throughout the country. By the time Lovell was decided, the principle was well-established in the precedents, and, to my knowledge, unanimously so. The original meaning had made its way into well-settled doctrine and was then ratified by the Court in Lovell.

    In a recent development, the original meaning also fit with practice, which took place in the shadow of the law but which likely also affected the law. In the Framing era, many influential Americans published their views using the printing press, whether in pamphlets or as submissions to newspapers. It would be odd to think that they would have secured special constitutional rights to the just-emerging category of newspapermen, who were in some measure lower status than they were, while denying the same rights to themselves.

    Industry observers note that and though those newspapers became relatively more influential in the following centuries, a tradition of leafletting and pamphleteering continued. The Court in 1938 could see the media reality as well as media law and naturally view the nonprofessional leafletter as having the same free press rights as a professional newspaper editor.

    In a recent development, the very first case in which the Supreme Court struck down government action as violating constitutional rights of freedom of expression, Stromberg v. California (1931), involved neither the press nor speech in the literal sense. Rather, it involved what one might today call symbolic expression (or expressive conduct)—the display of a red flag as a revolutionary symbol.

    But the opinion never discussed why displaying a flag counted as "speech" or "press." The opinion below similarly assumed that symbolic expression was as protected as verbal expression, and so did the parties' briefs in the Supreme Court. The Court had neither before nor since analyzed whether this result is consistent with the original meaning of the free expression guarantees. {See Eugene Volokh, Symbolic Expression and the Original Meaning of the First Amendment, 97 Geo. L.J. 1057 (2009).}.

    Likewise, the 1920 California Supreme Court decision in Ex parte Hartman (1920) struck down an earlier law banning the possession or display of flags that represented efforts "espous[ing] for the government of … the United States of America … principles or theories of government antagonistic … to the form of the government thereof as now constituted." The court concluded that Americans have "the right to advocate peaceable changes in our Constitution, laws or form of government," and that therefore "an organization peaceably advocating such changes may adopt a flag … signifying its purpose, and that the display or possession of such flag … cannot be made an unlawful act." The court simply assumed that symbolic expression was constitutionally equivalent to verbal expression, without discussing the matter further.

    But while these assumptions weren't backed by any originalist analysis, they appear to have been fully consistent with the Framing-era understanding that symbolic expression, pictorial expression, and verbal expression were generally treated as functionally equivalent. This equivalence was most often drawn with regard to restrictions on expression, such as defamation law. But it was also the view taken in the early republic with regard to constitutional protections for expression.

    Recent findings suggest that thus, for instance, pre-Revolutionary libel law recognized the category of libel by "pictures, signs, and the like"—meaning through symbols, whether printed or physically displayed—as tantamount to libel by writing. Early American law did the same, extending the same principle to incitement to riot as well. Early treatises drew this equivalence. Early court decisions suggested that pictorial and symbolic expression was potentially protected by free expression guarantees (though subject to the same constitutionally permissible restrictions, such as libel law, as verbal expression).

    To offer a particularly vivid illustration, consider the report of Mezzara's Case (1817), apparently the earliest American case involving nonverbal libel—there, a painting of the plaintiff with donkey's ears. The reporter, a Latest York lawyer, followed the case with a note hypothesizing what would happen if the painting were an apt commentary on the subject's folly and lack of patriotism. In such a situation, the reporter wrote, "[I]f the painter could show the truth of the matter in evidence, as before described, and that he published and exhibited the picture, 'with good motives and for justifiable ends,' … would he not be justifiable under our statute?".

    The statute the reporter cites—which did allow truth as a defense in libel actions, if the defendant acted with good motives and for justifiable ends—was passed in the wake of the Upcoming York court's evenly dividing in People v. Croswell (1804) on whether the freedom of the press mandated that the defense of truth be allowed in libel prosecutions. The statute implemented Chancellor James Kent's view of the constitutional rule, which was also the view championed by Alexander Hamilton (as Croswell's lawyer) in one of the last public acts of his life, and was seen as an crucial protection for the liberty of the press. And just four years after Mezzara's Case, at the next New York constitutional convention, the statute's provisions were adopted as part of the New York Constitution.

    The reporter thus saw nothing odd in treating a painting as protected by free expression principles, just as the court saw nothing odd in treating a painting as punishable under libel law principles. Likewise, three-dimensional symbolic expression, such as the raising of a liberty pole, was similarly treated as being potentially constitutionally protected just as pictorial and verbal expression were (though again subject to the possible constitutional limitations imposed on verbal expression).

    Recent findings suggest that this equivalence of symbolic, pictorial, and verbal expression unsurprisingly endured as part of the law—most often discussed as to libel law—throughout the 1800s and early 1900s. The Supreme Court, for instance, mentioned in 1845 that libel was a "species of defamation which is effected by writing or printing, or by pictures and signs," and in 1904 quoted a law enacted by the Philippine Commission that offered the same definition. There had been hundreds of similar holdings from state courts, whether explicating the common law or state statutes (and often including "effigies" alongside pictures and signs). Legal treatises had set forth the same principle.

    Thus, again, when the cases came before the California Supreme Court in 1920 and the U.S. Supreme Court in 1931, it was natural for the courts and the litigants to casually assume that symbolic expression (there using flags) was likewise treated equivalently to verbal expression for purposes of freedom of expression law. What was accepted in the Framing era continued to be accepted, without any felt need for discussion, in the early 1900s. And here too this conclusion was supported by a long tradition of practice as well as doctrine: Symbolic expression (whether through effigies, processions, visual puns, and the like) was commonplace in the Framing era, and flags and other forms of symbols continued to be used the same way into the 1900s.

    Newly introduced York Times Co. v. Sullivan's "actual malice" requirement has of course been criticized as contrary to the original meaning of the First Amendment. But some have also criticized the case on the grounds that it improperly imports freedom of expression principles into civil tort liability. Here too the Court has never tried to explain this particular conclusion on originalist grounds. Likewise, none of the briefs in Sullivan made an originalist argument in favor of applying constitutional limitations to common law civil lawsuits.

    Nonetheless, here too this may have stemmed from the longstanding understanding, dating back to the Framing era, that freedom of expression guarantees did indeed potentially apply to civil liability. We see that starting with 1802 and 1806 decisions from the Vermont and South Carolina high courts, rejecting liability in part by citing the state equivalents of the Petition Clause. {See generally Eugene Volokh, Tort Liability and the Original Meaning of the Freedom of Speech, Press, and Petition, 96 Iowa L. Rev. 249 (2010) (discussing this).}  And we see that in other cases from 1799 onwards that reasoned that constitutional protections may apply to civil lawsuits as well as to criminal prosecutions, but that libelous speech was constitutionally unprotected against civil liability as well as against criminal punishment. Early commentators took the same view.

    Sources indicate that and here too the early original meaning turned into well-established constitutional tradition. Throughout the 1800s and 1900s, court decisions routinely assumed that constitutional protections could limit civil liability, though subject to the recognition that there was essentially a First Amendment libel exception for civil as well as criminal liability. By the time of Upcoming York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964), this position just wasn't particularly controversial, even if the other features of that decision were.

    In a recent development, the economy is growing strongly, so why is nobody hiring?The latest data show growth hit 3.4% in the third quarter of this year, faster than expected. The puzzle is low hiring combined with unemployment at only 4.2%, where it's been for pretty much a year and a half, while jobless claims are actually near historic lows.In other words, companies aren't firing workers; they're just not hiring fresh ones. That means firms are delaying new hires.The first casualties are recent college grads, especially those destined for America's cubicle farms.     The economy is growing strongly, so why is nobody hiring?

    It has been revealed that the latest data show growth hit 3.4% in the third quarter of this year, faster than expected. Yet during that same quarter, the economy only added about 50,000 jobs per month—basically flat in an economy of 330 million people.

    Betting markets are forecasting a small uptick: 70,000 last month, less than population growth, in a supposedly sizzling economy. The puzzle is low hiring combined with unemployment at only 4.2%, where it's been for pretty much a year and a half, while jobless claims are actually near historic lows.

    In other words, companies aren't firing workers; they're just not hiring newly introduced ones. That’s odd since booming GDP usually spawns jobs like mushrooms after rain. The reason could be artificial intelligence—“super intelligence,” if you didn't get the memo.

    It has been revealed that the theory is that AI isn't crushing jobs by the millions, but it’s encouraging companies to do more with the people they've got because the technology is providing massive productivity gains. That means firms are delaying new hires.

    The first casualties are recent college grads, especially those destined for America's cubicle farms. An August Stanford study found that employment among 22- to-25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations was almost 20% below low-exposed jobs, with that gap up by one-third in the last year.

    >>> What AI Means for the Future of Work.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, experienced workers have no gap—just the new hires. So it’s junior programmers, administrative assistants, entry-level analysts and the army of recent graduates whose job was to rearrange PowerPoint to entertain middle managers.

    Recent findings suggest that this is creating an interesting labor market where experienced workers are valuable because they're actually more efficient with AI, since it’s a force multiplier. But for those with no industry expertise, it’s multiplying zero, which means nothing.

    Industry observers note that that means newly introduced graduates can't get their initial workplace experience because AI replaced them before they even indicated up. So, AI's not taking all the jobs, but it is taking the first rung of the career ladder in certain sectors.

    We've seen this movie before. In 1900, half of American workers were employed in agriculture. Along came tractors and combines, and today it's less than 2%. Yet America didn't end up with 38% unemployment back then because the new machines freed agriculture workers to make cars and airplanes, and eventually to write software, be personal trainers and fill other jobs.

    It was the same story when computers eliminated typists, bookkeepers and clerks. Millions of jobs were simultaneously created in software, telecommunications, online commerce and fulfillment centers.

    Technology doesn't simply eliminate work. Rather, it makes workers more productive, lowers costs, increases purchasing power—so customers buy more stuff—and opens opportunities that didn't exist. The entire Keynesian notion of aggregate demand is a fallacy because humans have unlimited wants.

    >>> The Tale of the Disappearing Jobs Numbers.

    There will always be demand for more products and services, including things that haven’t been invented yet. The catch is that those newly introduced jobs don't appear automatically. Entrepreneurs have to create them, which is why Steve Jobs was such a visionary for inventing the smartphone.

    Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, the creation of new enterprises is where governments enter the story. Starting a business or hiring your first employee can mean licenses, zoning, permits, tax registrations, insurance mandates, payroll compliance, labor-law restrictions and more. It’s an obstacle course trying to crush the next wave of jobs.

    It has been revealed that these matter most to small companies, precisely from where the next generation of jobs should come. New business establishments already create roughly 4 million jobs a year. But imagine how much faster that’d be if starting a business or hiring an employee was like ordering a T-shirt on Amazon.

    Sources indicate that the solution isn't to ban technology any more than it was to ban tractors or electricity. It's to unleash tomorrow's entrepreneurs.

    It has been revealed that slash occupational licensing, payroll taxes, employment-law complexity, and strip away unnecessary permits and zoning. Make it easy to start a business, experiment and hire the first employee.

    According to recent reports, technology has been eliminating jobs for thousands of years. In fact, that's how we became rich—the industrial revolution wiping out farm laborers. But what we didn't have in 1840 was an empire of taxes and regulations roadblocking millions of upcoming jobs.

    If that doesn't change, this time will, in fact, be different.

    The Fed Got It Right; Now Congress Must Do the Same

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, every day, the federal government spends nearly $3 billion on interest on its debt.

    • When the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Oct.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, every day, the federal government spends nearly $3 billion on interest on its debt. That’s almost $120 million per hour—and it only covers the cost of past borrowing.When the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Oct. 28, many in Washington and across the country were hoping for a cut, but the Federal Open Market Committee kept its target range for the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00%.The Fed’s decision increases borrowing costs for families and businesses, weighing on everything from mortgages to business investment. There’s also an uncomfortable consequence for Washington: It makes financing an already enormous federal debt even more expensive.The U.S. national debt now exceeds $40 trillion, roughly 126% of GDP, and continues to climb. America’s national debt has skyrocketed eightfold in a quarter century, with no signs of slowing down.As the size of the debt grows, the cost of carrying it also increases. But that’s not an argument for easier monetary policy. It’s an argument for responsible fiscal policy.>>> No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase AffordabilityLast year, the U.S. collected $5.5 trillion in revenues and spent $7.5 trillion in outlays, running a $2 trillion deficit. Interest on the $40 trillion debt accounted for nearly $1.3 trillion of that spending. To finance deficits, the government borrows by issuing securities, primarily Treasury bills, notes, and bonds.When investors expect persistently higher inflation, they demand higher yields to compensate for the expected erosion of purchasing power. That pushes Treasury yields higher, making upcoming federal borrowing more expensive.With Washington already carrying $40 trillion in debt and persistently running large deficits, higher borrowing costs increase the government’s interest burden.The result is a doom loop cycle: substantial debt leads to higher interest costs, wider deficits, more borrowing, and still more debt.This is why the Federal Reserve acts, and not in the way Washington may prefer.The Fed doesn’t exist to keep the government’s borrowing costs low. Its “dual mandate” is to maximize total employment and maintain price stability. The Bureau of Economic Analysis estimated August 2026 inflation at 3.4%, still above the 2% stated target. This supports the Fed’s continued focus on curbing inflation and, more importantly, inflationary expectations.Demanding the Fed suppress interest rates to make borrowing cheaper merely attacks the symptom, not the disease. Though lower rates can address affordability concerns and ease pressure on federal deficits, restoring price stability will require higher interest rates for potentially longer periods once households and investors expect higher inflation.For long-term price stability, it was crucial that the Fed send the signal that it remains committed to protecting the purchasing power of the dollar, even when doing so comes at a short-term cost—namely interest payments.Interest on the national debt is expected to reach $2.1 trillion by fiscal 2036, making it the third-largest single-line item on the budget and nearly 20% of federal spending. The Congressional Budget Office projects annual federal deficits will rise from $1.9 trillion to $3.1 trillion in the next decade, partially driven by rising interest costs. The CBO also estimates that if interest rates were 1.5% above expectations, cumulative deficits would increase by $6.0 trillion, even if Congress doesn’t enact additional spending.>>> How to Thaw the Frozen Housing MarketLeft unchecked, rising rates and debt-service costs create an increasingly vicious fiscal cycle: more revenue goes toward servicing yesterday’s borrowing, leaving less room for today’s priorities and forcing Washington to borrow more. Eventually, policymakers face increasingly painful choices over taxes, spending, and entitlement reform.The Federal Reserve didn’t create Washington’s $40 trillion debt. Congress and leaders of both parties did. The Fed shouldn’t feel pressured to erase the consequences of decades of deficit spending by keeping interest rates artificially low. That responsibility falls on Congress.Lawmakers must put the federal budget on a sustainable long-term path toward balance. Ensuring generated revenues cover all non-interest spending, known as a “primary balance,” can be achieved by voting in representatives who support fiscal responsibility.Waste and fraud should be rooted out wherever they exist, but those savings cannot substitute for confronting the structural drivers of federal spending. The CBO projects that government spending on Social Security and Medicare, along with interest payments, will grow faster than the economy over the coming decade. Any serious fiscal proposal must acknowledge that.For decades, Democrats and Republicans seemingly agreed with unlimited spending and only disagreed over what it should be spent on. The Federal Reserve is not responsible for today’s fiscal problem or the solution. The Fed’s job is to protect the value of the dollar, not the value of Washington’s borrowing habit.The Fed got it right. Now Washington needs to do the same.

    In a recent development, every day, the federal government spends nearly $3 billion on interest on its debt. That’s almost $120 million per hour—and it only covers the cost of past borrowing.

    When the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Oct. 28, many in Washington and across the country were hoping for a cut, but the Federal Open Market Committee kept its target range for the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00%.

    The Fed’s decision increases borrowing costs for families and businesses, weighing on everything from mortgages to business investment. There’s also an uncomfortable consequence for Washington: It makes financing an already enormous federal debt even more expensive.

    The U.S. national debt now exceeds $40 trillion, roughly 126% of GDP, and continues to climb. The last time the federal government recorded a budget surplus was in 2001 when the debt was only $5 trillion. America’s national debt has skyrocketed eightfold in a quarter century, with no signs of slowing down.

    According to recent reports, as the size of the debt grows, the cost of carrying it also increases. But that’s not an argument for easier monetary policy. It’s an argument for responsible fiscal policy.

    >>> No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase Affordability.

    Last year, the U.S. collected $5.5 trillion in revenues and spent $7.5 trillion in outlays, running a $2 trillion deficit. Interest on the $40 trillion debt accounted for nearly $1.3 trillion of that spending. To finance deficits, the government borrows by issuing securities, primarily Treasury bills, notes, and bonds.

    Sources indicate that when investors expect persistently higher inflation, they demand higher yields to compensate for the expected erosion of purchasing power. That pushes Treasury yields higher, making upcoming federal borrowing more expensive.

    With Washington already carrying $40 trillion in debt and persistently running large deficits, higher borrowing costs increase the government’s interest burden.

    The result is a doom loop cycle: substantial debt leads to higher interest costs, wider deficits, more borrowing, and still more debt.

    This is why the Federal Reserve acts, and not in the way Washington may prefer.

    In a recent development, the Fed doesn’t exist to keep the government’s borrowing costs low. Its “dual mandate” is to maximize total employment and maintain price stability. The Bureau of Economic Analysis estimated August 2026 inflation at 3.4%, still above the 2% stated target. This supports the Fed’s continued focus on curbing inflation and, more importantly, inflationary expectations.

    Sources indicate that demanding the Fed suppress interest rates to make borrowing cheaper merely attacks the symptom, not the disease. Though lower rates can address affordability concerns and ease pressure on federal deficits, restoring price stability will require higher interest rates for potentially longer periods once households and investors expect higher inflation.

    For long-term price stability, it was crucial that the Fed send the signal that it remains committed to protecting the purchasing power of the dollar, even when doing so comes at a short-term cost—namely interest payments.

    Interest on the national debt is expected to reach $2.1 trillion by fiscal 2036, making it the third-largest single-line item on the budget and nearly 20% of federal spending. The Congressional Budget Office projects annual federal deficits will rise from $1.9 trillion to $3.1 trillion in the next decade, partially driven by rising interest costs. The CBO also estimates that if interest rates were 1.5% above expectations, cumulative deficits would increase by $6.0 trillion, even if Congress doesn’t enact additional spending.

    >>> How to Thaw the Frozen Housing Market.

    It has been revealed that left unchecked, rising rates and debt-service costs create an increasingly vicious fiscal cycle: more revenue goes toward servicing yesterday’s borrowing, leaving less room for today’s priorities and forcing Washington to borrow more. Eventually, policymakers face increasingly painful choices over taxes, spending, and entitlement reform.

    Recent findings suggest that the Federal Reserve didn’t create Washington’s $40 trillion debt. Congress and leaders of both parties did. The Fed shouldn’t feel pressured to erase the consequences of decades of deficit spending by keeping interest rates artificially low. That responsibility falls on Congress.

    Sources indicate that lawmakers must put the federal budget on a sustainable long-term path toward balance. Ensuring generated revenues cover all non-interest spending, known as a “primary balance,” can be achieved by voting in representatives who support fiscal responsibility.

    Waste and fraud should be rooted out wherever they exist, but those savings cannot substitute for confronting the structural drivers of federal spending. The CBO projects that government spending on Social Security and Medicare, along with interest payments, will grow faster than the economy over the coming decade. Any serious fiscal initiative must acknowledge that.

    For decades, Democrats and Republicans seemingly agreed with unlimited spending and only disagreed over what it should be spent on. The Federal Reserve is not responsible for today’s fiscal problem or the solution. The Fed’s job is to protect the value of the dollar, not the value of Washington’s borrowing habit.

    According to recent reports, the Fed got it right. Now Washington needs to do the same.

    💡 Key Takeaways
