    #8924. Latest Update: Christina Henry on translating the unexpected horrors of motherhood into fiction

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1385 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Christina Henry on translating the unexpected horrors of motherhood into fiction

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1385 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that we all have a picture in our head of a mother—what we think a mother should be or shouldn’t be, what ideal motherhood looks like.
    • But being a mother, or a stepmother, or a mother figure, is hard.
    • According to recent reports, once your child is born you might think, Great, it’s going to be nothing but sunshine and roses from here on out.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that we all have a picture in our head of a mother—what we think a mother should be or shouldn’t be, what ideal motherhood looks like. Society creates expectations for mothers, and mothers who color outside those lines are often censured by those around them.

    But being a mother, or a stepmother, or a mother figure, is hard. If you carry a child you might think that pregnancy will be nine months of glowing, radiant bliss (that’s what all those parenting influencers say on TikTok, don’t they?) Instead, you’re coping with swollen feet and sciatica, and the constant worry that you might do something that will accidentally harm your growing baby.

    According to recent reports, once your child is born you might think, Great, it’s going to be nothing but sunshine and roses from here on out. But parenting isn’t just drippy ice cream cones on the beach and smiling while riding carousels. There are so many things you can’t anticipate—unexpected illnesses, trouble at school, headstrong kids who simply want their own way.

    According to recent reports, the truth of the matter that having a child and raising a child are often some of the most anxiety-riddled years of a person’s life. Even when nothing’s going wrong, a mother can often feel like something just might go wrong. The worry they are feeling is somehow a hedge against bad things happening—parental anxiety as a shield against actual harm.

    It has been revealed that fictional mothers, of course, get the worst of it. It’s bad enough that real-world mothers have to cope with spiking fevers and school permission forms and judgmental in-laws. But what if you desperately want a child but it turns out your baby was also, say, the son of Satan? Or what if you love your children with all your heart but you keep hearing things, seeing things that you aren’t sure are actually there? What if the people around you aren’t to be trusted? What if you feel like you can’t trust yourself?

    Everyone knows about Rosemary, right? Poor Rosemary Woodhouse, whose gaslighting jerk of a husband, Guy, trades her womb for a successful career.

    In Ira Levin’s classic novel of motherhood horror, Rosemary’s Baby, Rosemary is a cheery newlywed who wants to have a child. Guy is a struggling actor who keeps just missing his substantial break and wants to wait a little longer to start a family. A bit of timely luck allows them to sign a lease in an older building called the Bramford, a place that’s notoriously difficult to get into. Rosemary is thrilled that, at least, she will have the decoration of a new place to keep her busy, but she still wishes for a baby.

    Recent findings suggest that an older couple, Roman and Minnie Castavet, live in the next apartment. Rosemary finds them nosy and annoying, but for some reason Guy likes them and starts to visit regularly. Then, a miracle happens. The actor who cast in a role that Guy almost got is suddenly struck blind (a miracle for Guy, of course, not so much for the other actor) and Guy lands a role that can make his career. Soon after this unexpectedly fortuitous occurrence, he decides that he does, in fact, want a baby.

    Shortly after, Rosemary has a terrible dream—a dream about a beast who rapes her while several people look on. And then, the second miracle happens. Rosemary is pregnant. Except her pregnancy doesn’t feel right, and everyone around her keeps telling her it’s fine.

    Rosemary’s journey is so harrowing because no matter what she says or does or even knows with absolute certainty, no one will believe her. If you’ve never read this one it’s time to give it a try.

    Recent findings suggest that kit Burgoyne’s The Captive is a clever play on the I’ve-been-impregnated-by-Satan-against-my-will story, or in this case, by an entity alternately referred to as “The Long-Before” or “Him.” An underground revolutionary group that call themselves the Nail decide to kidnap Adeline Woolsaw, the wealthy heiress of a vast network of connected businesses, in hopes of exposing the Woolsaws and their corruption to the public. The only time Adeline ever seems to leave the vast estate where she lives is to go to the doctor’s office, so the group decides to grab her as she leaves her appointment.

    Unfortunately for the Nail, Adeline is pregnant. Even more unfortunately, Adeline is going into labor in the van. Just to add to their confusion, Adeline most definitely does not want to return home to her parents. It seems that her parents worship this evil entity and arranged to have Adeline carry His child in order to establish total world domination.

    This pitch-black story skewers the cultists, the radical revolutionaries and the oligarchs that run everything equally and mashes it all up into a super-fun (and frequently gory) thriller.

    Industry observers note that helen Phillip’s The Need is probably one of my favorite novels of the last ten years. I’ve never read another book that so accurately embodies both the intense love of a mother for her children and also the profound, dragging monotony of the daily tasks that make up her day.

    Molly is a mom of two and a paleobotanist, alone with the kids while her partner travels. She is exhausted, exhausted in that bone-deep way parents often are, feeling like she wants to stay on top of everything but she simply cannot.

    It has been revealed that when she hears footsteps in her home she thinks she’s imagining them. She’s anxious about a potential home invasion. She can’t trust herself. She’s just sleep-deprived. But then she comes face to face with an intruder wearing a mask, and the reality of Molly’s world tilts precariously on its side.

    The less you know about this one, the better. It unfolds like a strange and fascinating puzzle box, revealing layers as it goes.

    Recent findings suggest that neena Viel’s debut Listen to Your Sister isn’t about a mother, per se. But it is about Calla Williams, a twenty-five-year-old woman just trying to keep it together, who reluctantly agrees to become the guardian to her sixteen-year-old brother Jamie. Jamie, like most 16-year-olds, is not interested in his sister’s authority, or any kind of authority, really. Their brother Dre agreed to help Calla with Jamie, but he has his own struggles and isn’t exactly present.

    Calla keeps trying, keeps sacrificing, keeps muddling along trying to do her best like every mother figure. Ever since her brothers were young she’s had visions of their dying in horrible ways, and her nightmares stoke her anxiety over their well-being. But her resentment is growing. No matter how much she loves her brothers, they don’t seem to love her enough to change.

    Industry observers note that one day Jamie’s behavior goes a little too far and the siblings are forced to flee their homes to hide out at a cabin in the woods. It’s there that Calla’s patience finally snaps, and her brothers discover that the nightmares Calla has had all their lives might just be real.

    Neena Viel’s writing is so intense, so profoundly visual, that this book has been indelibly imprinted on my brain. I’m still thinking about it months later.

    In my own upcoming novel Pinfeathers, stay-at-home mom Nora Pacetti is tired and frustrated that her husband, Adam, isn’t keeping up his end of the parenting bargain. But those problems seem trivial once Nora discovers a strange object sticking out of her baby’s arm.

    In a recent development, nora thinks it must be a splinter. But when she examines it closely the object seems to have come through her daughter’s skin, not pierced it from the outside. Then Nora’s mother Giulia looks at it and renders her verdict—it’s a pinfeather, a baby feather.

    Nora doesn’t know what to believe, and then she finds another one. Does her daughter have a strange disease, or is she actually turning into a bird?

    Christina Henry is the author of The Mermaid, Lost Boy, Alice, Red Queen, and the national bestselling Black Wings series featuring Agent of Death Madeline Black and her popcorn-loving gargoyle, Beezle.

    Guess what Rotten Tomatoes states is the best James Bond movie?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It’s the grading system of Rotten Tomatoes dot com, a website where movie criticism is treated like a report card.
    • In a recent development, I have my concerns with Rotten Tomatoes (beginning with the mere practice of converting a critique into a numbered score) … but that website and I do agree on one thing.
    • It has been revealed that the website has ranked all twenty-seven James Bond films (the twenty-five real ones and the two impostors), according to their Tomatometer score, which is a rating out of 100.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You’ve heard of the tomatometer. It’s the grading system of Rotten Tomatoes dot com, a website where movie criticism is treated like a report card.

    In a recent development, I have my concerns with Rotten Tomatoes (beginning with the mere practice of converting a critique into a numbered score) … but that website and I do agree on one thing. And that’s the best James Bond movie of all time.

    It has been revealed that the website has ranked all twenty-seven James Bond films (the twenty-five real ones and the two impostors), according to their Tomatometer score, which is a rating out of 100. That score is the average of all the numerical scores it has received from film critics (meaning that critics’ reviews have been transformed into numbers out of 100 that seem to capture their sentiments, just like getting a grade from a teacher on an essay).

    What does it reveal is the best?

    In a recent development, goldfinger, which has a 99% rating on the site. This happens to be correct.

    1967’s Casino Royale, a film which is so tremendously bad I don’t recommend you see it even if you’re wondering “how bad could it be?” That has a ranking of 28%, says the Tomatometer. Which also feels pretty correct.

    But that’s not a real Bond film, so we have to look to the penultimate ranked film to know which Rotten Tomatoes has revealed is the “worst” Bond film. And that’s 1985’s A View to a Kill starring Roger Moore, Grace Jones, and Christopher Walken, which has a 38%.

    You can check out the rest of the rankings here.

    (I, personally, find it perplexing that Never Say Never Again ranks so well, but then again, I’m only one person, not the mean of all the film critics who wrote something about it.).

    It has been revealed that olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. She hosts the podcasst "Culture Schlock" at Lit Hub Radio. She is on instagram at @oldebean, twitter at @oldrutigliano, and bluesky at @oliviarutigliano.bsky.social.

You'll build that motion rather than inherit it.

    In a recent development, success is measured in dollars: gross revenue retention in your cohort first, expansion second. Not tickets closed, not calls booked.

    #8919. 5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1066 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Adjectives like streetwise and street-smart exist to acknowledge the specific intelligence needed to navigate the perils of urban living.
    • There’s plenty of menace in small places.
    • I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You expect danger in the city. Adjectives like streetwise and street-smart exist to acknowledge the specific intelligence needed to navigate the perils of urban living. Country intelligence has no succinct adjectives. Country-strong, that’s a thing. But, country-wise? More often than not, there is a misconception that life in the hinterlands will dull your edge, diminish your reflexes, lull you into a false sense of security.

    There’s plenty of menace in small places. In towns with no interstate ramp, nameless desert stops with no cell phone service, a desperate farm community surrounded by an ocean of corn.

    I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors. These don’t have to be set in the South—mine are—but they can happen anywhere. Maybe it’s Southern noir when done south of the Mason-Dixon line. Rural noir is a good name, and throws its arms around the whole genre, but it’s a mouthful. It comes out sounding slurry, even when I’m sober, and might not come out at all if I’ve had a cocktail. This subgenre of crime fiction goes by many names. I wish I could just tell people I wrote Southerns and have them understand—the way most people understand the Western. Till then, here are five of my favorite examples of novels that take place out past the last lights of town.

    Industry observers note that vital note: I had to leave out a lot of authors I adore and beg you to read anything and everything by the following for outstanding examples of small-town, insular, tight-nit, and Sun-Belt crime: Flannery O’Connor, S.A. Cosby, Carson McCullers, Henry Wise, Attica Locke, Dennis Lehane, Megan Abbott, Ivy Pochoda, and Elmore Leonard. Please find them.

    Daniel Woodrell is incredible. I love every word he has ever written but Tomato Red is my favorite. It opens with a gorgeous run-on sentence that’s almost three hundred words long and, after reading it, it’s almost impossible not to collapse and read the whole book in one sitting. The novel’s hapless anti-hero, Sammy Barlach—recently fired from a dog food factory and fresh off a speed-fueled burglary attempt—throws in with siblings Jason and Jamalee Merridew. Jason, a local object of female obsession, and his sister Jamalee want to weaponize Jason’s beauty, blackmail wealthy woman, and get them both out of Venus Holler. Sammy hitches his wagon to the Merridew’s scheme. But for Jason, a gay man in the hills and hollows of the Ozarks, choosing to live an authentic life proves to me more dangerous than one of crime.

    One of my favorite sayings from Tod Goldberg is that he writes about bad people doing terrible things to even worse people. In The Low Desert, he demonstrates this across twelve sometimes-connected stories set on the outskirts of California and Nevada. There are lonely deserts, fading resort towns, lost highways. Each story is a banger, but the fact that Goon Number Four isn’t your favorite TV show of the last decade is a miscarriage of justice. A story about a hired gun who enrolls in a community college, seeking to be rid of the life, only to find exploitation waiting in the halls of normalcy. The Low Desert has something I have never been able to fully articulate—feeling more like a great album, than the seminal work of crime fiction it is.

    A personal favorite, Thompson’s Pop. 1280 is a novel that perfectly balances menace and comedy. Nick Corey, a terrible sheriff, oversees the 1280 souls of Potts County, Texas. Many of Nick’s constituents don’t want a sheriff, prefer to skirt the law, and tolerate him because he is pathologically shiftless. Our sheriff eats five meals a day, sleeps with any woman who’s up for it, sees murder as the only option rather than a last resort, and will do anything to keep his job. Not because he is ambitious, but because being sheriff allows him to do almost nothing. But, on the precipice of a difficult reelection, he reluctantly springs into action. Through the ensuing morass, Nick confronts sassy pimps, his pushy wife and her brother, his mistress and her husband, the town as whole, and the very concept of righteousness. Corey is a man who seems dumb, but isn’t. Someone dangerous and ruthless in the most peculiar and befuddling ways.

    Cormac McCarthy, No Country for Old Men.

    Cormac McCarthy’s most accessible novel. It is a literary crime novel that dissects the corrosive effects of money, heightened to break-neck entertainment by the inclusion of one of fiction’s most unforgettable bad dudes. In many ways, this is Anton Chigurh’s book the way Jaws belongs to the shark. Chigurh, a relentless hitman who’s as dangerous to his employers as he is to his targets, is evil with biblical scope. Ed-Tom Bell is a good man fading. A sheriff having and existential crisis, struggling to adapt to the requirements of his calling in a world where criminality has moved past opportunism and into something inconceivable. Throw in Llewelyn Moss, a Vietnam vet who stumbles across two million dollars after a drug deal goes wrong, and you’re in for a ride. When Chigurh’s tide of malevolence come in. One man tries to stem it, the other retreats. Fates are decided by the flip of a coin.

    Frank Bill, Crimes in Southern Indiana.

    Sources indicate that frank Bill’s debut, Crimes in Southern Indiana, is a cold look at a brutal version of Indiana that exists off the interstates. Southern Indiana is an anomaly—not quite the South, not quite the Midwest. Claimed by none—like the folks Bill writes about. He drops seventeen stories about this distinct region across two hundred and seventy pages in an achingly authentic voice. He can do more damage in ten pages than most other savvy word-geeks could with a lifetime supply of paper. The Penance of Scoot McCutchen will wreck you. I think about it all the time.

    Ty Landers holds an MFA in Creative Writing and Writing for the Performing Arts from the University of California, Riverside. Born and raised in Alabama, he spent more than twenty years in Nashville, Tennessee, before moving to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, with his wife and sons. His debut novel BABY QUEEN, out on November 17, 2026, is being adapted by HBO. For more on Ty Landers, visit: https://www.tylandersfiction.com/.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 11, 2026, 12:14 pm CST.

    According to Law.com, the next phase will center on paying creditors—chiefly landlords—and collecting outstanding receivables. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    Partners at Weil, Gotshal & Manges have formally voted to dissolve the nearly century-old law firm.

    Law.com reported Tuesday that 97% of the firm’s partners approved the move, which came about two weeks after the management committee recommended it Oct. 28. A three-person dissolution committee will oversee the firm’s dissolution, while Weil Gotshal executive chair Barry Wolf will act as a special consultant through the end of the year and longer if the wind-down runs into 2027. The firm will also utilize restructuring officers from management consulting agency AlixPartners and Davis Polk & Wardwell.

    According to Law.com, the next phase will center on paying creditors—chiefly landlords—and collecting outstanding receivables.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, Law.com added that Weil Gotshal restructuring chair Matt Barr and several bankruptcy lawyers are in advanced talks to join Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, which would remove one of Weil Gotshal’s last high-performing groups. Neither Barr nor Skadden responded to Law.com’s requests for comment.

    Recent findings suggest that barr’s potential move would be the latest in a partner exodus that has helped bring down the once-venerated Wall Street firm. According to Law.com, the firm saw nearly 50 partner exits in 2026, with sources estimating at least $500 million in lost business.

    Rivals race to rescue Weil Gotshal lawyers as firm heads toward closure.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media.
    • Sources indicate that on Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state.
    • “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media. Let alone the international news media. But during the traditionally slow Christmas holiday, when even serious outlets stoop to tracking Santa’s progress across the northern hemisphere and presenting expert commentary on decorations at the White House, the story about the bodies found in the backwoods of the Pacific Northwest arrived like a Christmas gift from News Kringle.

    Sources indicate that on Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state. After a three-day search that involved more than sixty volunteers from two states, dogs, drones, and helicopters working through harsh terrain, icy conditions, and a snowstorm, their frozen bodies were recovered. On December 28, Portland’s CBS television affiliate KOIN 6 was among the first to pick up the story.

    “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.

    It has been revealed that did someone say Sasquatch? Every editor in the world knew clickbait when they saw it. Within days, near-identical headlines appeared around the world, backed by the biggest names in news.

    CNN: 2 Oregon men die from exposure in a forest after they went out to look for Sasquatch.

    Fox News: 2 dead after search for Sasquatch in Washington national forest.

    NPR: 2 men were found dead from exposure after looking for Sasquatch.

    BBC: Two men found dead while searching for Bigfoot.

    Nine News Australia: Two men found dead in US after going on Christmas Eve hunt for Bigfoot.

    It has been revealed that hundreds, perhaps thousands, jumped in. The Associated Press. MSN. CBS News. HuffPost. Newsweek. Today. Yahoo News. USA Today. New York Post. Los Angeles Times. San Francisco Chronicle. The Times. Daily Mail.

    In a recent development, the story was such a surefire traffic pusher that even specialized outlets ran with it. People. Sports Illustrated. AccuWeather. The celebrity and entertainment website TooFab. Spain’s national sports tabloid Marca. New Zealand’s Stuff. Taiwanese tabloid CTWant. The massively popular 52hrtt, a Chinese-language website that serves the global Chinese diaspora.

    There was no video, so each outlet looped the same images from a package of photos released by the Skamania County 23 sasquatch country Sheriff’s Office: four SAR volunteers on a snow-covered trail carrying an extension ladder through the forest; six volunteers in safety-orange jackets and helmets, one pointing a finger into the woods, using an extension ladder laid on the ground to cross a stream; a guy on hands and knees crawling across the ladder over a stream; a group of seven searchers using downed logs to cross a stream; and a Coast Guard helicopter hovering above an opening in the forest canopy.

    In a digitally powered echo chamber, local, regional, national, and international outlets repeated the story almost word for word. All the way across the continent, News Center Maine television led its December 30 national news roundup in typical fashion:.

    Sources indicate that we’ll start in Washington state. Two men were found dead there after going on a search for Bigfoot. They went out on their search a few days before Christmas Eve. When they didn’t return, family members contacted police. They were found after a three-day search. Local authorities there say it seems as though they likely died of exposure because of the weather conditions at the time and not being prepared.

    Sasquatch hunters. Christmas search. Poorly prepared. Died of exposure. That was all anyone seemed to know.

    In fact, those elementary pieces of the story were all anyone in the news media actually did know. As even a cursory examination of the torrent of articles and broadcasts about the two bodies found in the forest highlighted, the stories were noteworthy mostly for their striking uniformity and lack of information. But something about the story wasn’t right. Something didn’t add up.

    Industry observers note that the rule that credible journalists are meant to follow is that the details in a story must support its headline—particularly if that headline makes an audacious claim. Two guys froze to death while looking for Bigfoot? Wow. Bring on the details.

    In a recent development, but that was the thing about the story of the Christmas Sasquatch hunters. After the stun-gun heds and ledes, there were no details about the supposed Sasquatch hunt. Not scant details. Not vague details. No details whatsoever. As if by mandate, every outlet that picked up the story made sure to include Sasquatch in its headline and opening grab. Then they dropped the Bigfoot angle altogether.

    How long had the men been out looking for Sasquatch? Did they have a track record as Sasquatch hunters? Were they carrying special equipment, such as video cameras, long-range microphones, or telephoto lenses? If they were out searching for Sasquatch in rugged terrain and winter conditions, why were they so ill prepared?

    On these and other questions related to the Sasquatch hunt teased in the headlines, every story was the same—strangely mute.

    Excerpted from Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the New American Wilderness by Chuck Thompson via Counterpoint Press.

    Chuck Thompson is the longtime editor of Columbia Insight, an award-winning environmental and outdoor news website based in Hood River, Oregon, just across the Columbia River from Skamania County and the Gifford Pinchot National Forest. A former executive producer with CNN.com, deputy editor of Men’s Journal, and Outside magazine contributor, he’s the author The Status Revolution: The Improbable Story of How the Lowbrow Became the Highbrow; the widely reviewed political screed Better Off Without ’Em: A Northern Manifesto for Southern Secession; the acclaimed travel memoir Smile When You’re Lying: Confessions of a Rogue Travel Writer; and Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the Fresh American Wilderness.

    #8913. 5 gloriously unhinged speculative mysteries and thrillers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1148 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    5 gloriously unhinged speculative mysteries and thrillers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When a reviewer raved about my upcoming thriller, The Sleeper, with the words, “I love whatever is wrong with her,” I was delighted.
    • But this is not a modern phenomenon, there is a rich literary tradition of wild and crazy thrillers.
    • Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When a reviewer raved about my upcoming thriller, The Sleeper, with the words, “I love whatever is wrong with her,” I was delighted. It’s my eighth book. With each one I’ve taken a bigger, bolder, and yes, a more unhinged swing. And I’m not alone. There is a rabid pack of unhinged thriller writers out there, and we’re only getting more bananas.

    But this is not a modern phenomenon, there is a rich literary tradition of wild and crazy thrillers. In fact, I’ve found it incredibly hard to whittle this list down to just five. This list bounces between the newly introduced, the nearly new and the really rather old.

    Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.

    Industry observers note that one of those novels so powerful that it becomes a conceptual byword (by-phrase?) used even by people who have never read it. Published in 1886 and so brisk it’s actually a novella, this unflinching gothic masterpiece still holds its own in 2026.

    In a recent development, there is almost as much mythology about the writing of the book as is contained in its pages. Stevenson claimed that it sprang from a wild nightmare that contained three scenes and the central idea, “of a voluntary change becoming involuntary.” His step-son claimed it was written in a three-day fit of pique. His wife claimed that Stephenson burned the first version after she suggested he was writing an allegory, which riled him up before he realized he agreed, and then started again.

    Stephenson’s health at the time was dire, he was on medication to stop his lungs hemorrhaging, which could have stimulated the originating nightmare. According to some rumors he was also taking cocaine, which could also explain the mad work rate and agitation….

    If you haven’t read it recently (or perhaps ever), you may raise an eyebrow at its inclusion in a list of thrillers but it more than earns its place.

    Recent findings suggest that we have unreliable characters, memory blackouts, dual personalities and a race to stop a killer. And it’s actually, I would argue, a speculative thriller given that the whole problem starts with Dr Jekyll experimenting to create a serum that can overcome the dark parts of his personality. Instead, the serum splits him into two—the good Dr Jekyll, and the evil Mr Hyde.

    Sarah Pinborough, Behind Her Eyes.

    I know this came out nearly ten years ago but I’m still agape at its twists. Sarah Pinborough tore up the rule book with this one, and proved that you could still find fresh ways to shock a savvy audience of thriller readers.

    In a recent development, if you’ve not read it, I don’t want to give anything away but what starts as a tense psychological thriller about a single mum having an affair with her boss while forming a close friendship with the boss’s wife, soon takes a hard swerve into lucid dreaming, astral projection and a past timeline exploring trauma and mental illness. And if that sounds heavy and gloomy, I’m doing it a massive disservice because it is an absolute rollercoaster.

    The ending was so WILD that it was a key part of the marketing, with the hashtag #WTFthatending spreading through Book Twitter (this was 2017, after all…).

    Lisa Jewell, None Of This Is True.

    As a long-term fan, I loved watching the queen of women’s fiction become the doyenne of domestic suspense before winding her way down an ever-darker garden path. But Lisa Jewell’s 2023 novel, None Of This Is True, was a real escalation.

    It has been revealed that A fever dream of lies, paranoia and platonic limerence. Alix is a successful true crime podcaster who meets her “birthday twin,” Josie, an unassuming local woman born on the same day but whose life is very different.

    In a recent development, they both have secrets, of course, which I’m loathe to give away but the novel is unflinching around dark topics like grooming, alcoholism and family dysfunction. For all its sucker punches (and the twists are *brain exploding emoji*) this is a nuanced and heartfelt exploration of the stories we tell ourselves in order to survive.

    If you were an unemployed gambling addict unable to pay your debts and whose loved ones were being threatened by the Yakuza, you’d take the first well-paid job that comes your way too, right? In this case, as a private chef to a reclusive billionaire in remote Japan.

    Soon, protagonist Ed is somewhat learning on the job in the best kitchen money can buy at the heart of an enormous mansion, with an endless supply of whatever ingredients the esoteric tastes of his boss desires….

    It’s been likened to Butter by Asako Yuzuki and there are overlaps in themes of greed, obsession and—of course—murder, but while Butter is a slow burn, Greedy is a runaway train. Messy, freaky and eye wateringly gory. I mean all those things as compliments!

    Fiona Cummins, Serial Killer Survivors Club.

    While 1980s teenager Robyn reels from the discovery that her father was a serial killer, her life is made infinitely worse by community ostracism and judgement.

    Sources indicate that an experimental therapy group for the familial survivors of murderers changes her life, finally giving her the acceptance and friendship she has always craved. But when one of her latest friends disappears in a town where three other young women are already missing, Robyn and her found-family risk everything to find them. After all, with their intimate knowledge of killers, the Serial Killer Survivors Club are the best hope these missing women have….

    I pat myself on the back for my ability to predict twists but this one spun me for a total loop. I was lucky enough to grab an advanced readers copy of this, which will be published next year in the UK and US. I highly recommend pre-ordering.

    My own unhinged thriller, The Sleeper, follows librarian Maya who falls asleep on a sleeper train and wakes up in a version of the world where history has changed overnight, her own life has been erased and nobody remembers her.

    And the version of Britain she’s now living in? Just saying the wrong things can put you in the crosshairs of the state. Which is a massive problem for Maya, who in her bewilderment, has asked way too many questions already….

    Sources indicate that holly Seddon is the author of several thrillers, including the international bestseller Try Not to Breathe, The Hit List, and 59 Minutes. After growing up in the English countryside obsessed with music and books, Holly worked in London as a journalist and editor. After several years in Amsterdam, she now lives in Kent with her family and writes full time. Find out more at HollySeddon.com.

    #8912. Tech Report: Sacha Naspini on the human stories behind Italy’s tomb-raider subculture.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2215 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Sacha Naspini on the human stories behind Italy’s tomb-raider subculture.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bardo Sacchetti has the people of the Val di Cornia wrapped around his little finger.
    • When Bardo suddenly disappears, his son, Veleno, takes over the family business and old relationships between the gang and the milieu in which it operates begin to fray.
    • It has been revealed that sacha Naspini’s compact and suspenseful new novel, The Witch’s Mouth (2026, Europa, translated by Clarissa Botsford), drops you in the midst of the action, and creates a world peopled with crooks and cooks, a prostitute, heir-apparent, fishmonger, marquis.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tuscany, 1972. Bardo Sacchetti has the people of the Val di Cornia wrapped around his little finger. Thanks to him and his band of tomb raiders, locals in the impoverished region can now buy fridges for their homes or give their kids an education. He asks for nothing in return except for gratitude.

    When Bardo suddenly disappears, his son, Veleno, takes over the family business and old relationships between the gang and the milieu in which it operates begin to fray. Former alliances fall apart and Bardo’s empire looks like it might be destroyed by violence. Veleno has some big decisions to make.

    It has been revealed that sacha Naspini’s compact and suspenseful new novel, The Witch’s Mouth (2026, Europa, translated by Clarissa Botsford), drops you in the midst of the action, and creates a world peopled with crooks and cooks, a prostitute, heir-apparent, fishmonger, marquis. The story unfolds from their perspectives.

    I sent written questions to Naspini, and Edoardo Andreoni translated his written responses from Italian into English. The interview has been edited for length.

    Radha Vatsal: Let’s start with some background. Tuscany, where the novel takes place, seems to be littered with antiquities. Is this more the case in Tuscany than in other parts of Italy? Can you describe some of the types of antiquities that have been found there in recent years?

    In a recent development, sacha Naspini: Actually, that’s true of pretty much all of Italy. It’s a country where history has accumulated over millennia, layer upon layer. Here, even a routine excavation can turn into an archaeological discovery.

    Tuscany is no exception. In fact, it’s one of the regions where this historical layering is particularly evident, largely thanks to the Etruscan civilization, which preceded Roman rule. Discoveries are still being made today. Take the recent finds at San Casciano dei Bagni, near Siena: extraordinary bronzes, along with coins, crowns, jewelry, votive arms and heads….

    In a recent development, as for The Witch’s Mouth, the novel is set in a specific part of Tuscany, the Val di Cornia. It’s an area I know well, one that plays an key role in the fictional universe of some of my novels. This was once home to Populonia, one of the most important Etruscan cities and the only one built directly on the coast. In the Gulf of Baratti, you can visit Etruscan necropolises, monumental tombs, burial chambers carved into the rock, and the remains of Etruscan and Roman settlements.

    RV: The events in the novel occur in the early 1970s. Was there a particular reason for choosing this time period?

    It has been revealed that SN: Yes, there is. Choosing this period was an exciting challenge, and one that felt necessary. The Witch’s Mouth was born out of long conversations with tomb raiders and smugglers who were active during that time. Suddenly I came across some truly extraordinary, almost unbelievable stories. That’s when I began thinking about using this material as the basis for a novel.

    There were also three aspects that I found particularly fascinating. First of all, the “fever” I always noticed in the people who told me about their adventures. That’s the expression they would use: “digging fever.” It went beyond money or swashbuckling adventure—a special light would sparkle in their eyes. As these small-town Indiana Jones recalled those times, that almost addictive excitement was rekindled— the excitement of the moment when, after devising a initiative, they would finally manage to break into a burial site, the first people to set foot there in millennia. And then reach out and touch the objects… Part of my job was to try to capture their passion.

    The second aspect was even more intriguing and had to do specifically with the Val di Cornia. The trafficking of archaeological artifacts was already underway in other parts of Italy—for instance in the Tuscia region—but in this small corner of Tuscany, people were late to the game.

    I heard crazy stories of farmers whose cellars were filled with bronzes that had turned up when they were plowing the land, and who would give them to their grandchildren to play with, like toy soldiers. After storms at sea, amphorae would wash up on the shore at Baratti. Kids would place them on top of low walls and throw rocks at them. Women would show up at Mass on Sunday wearing earrings and necklaces found in the fields….

    So I wondered, what would happen if an entire community, largely made up of people who struggle to make ends meet, suddenly realized that their homes were full of objects they considered worthless but that could fetch millions on the black market?

    As I was researching the historical archives of the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, I came across a news story from 1971 about a twelve-inch bronze artifact seized by the Carabinieri. It was about to be sold to an American collector for half a billion lire (roughly $5 million in today’s money). People in that region had piles of similar bronzes, tossed aside in a corner.

    Finally, a purely personal aspect. I spent part of my childhood and adolescence in that region. Other kids and I would form our own little gangs and sneak out of the house in the middle of the night armed, with ropes, shovels, and spades, and head off into the woods. We imagined we were living in The Goonies, but instead of searching for One-Eyed Willy’s treasure, we were searching for Etruscan artifacts. Thinking back on it, what mattered wasn’t so much finding something as the adventure itself. Entering the woods at night was a big challenge. And then the thrill of digging, without really knowing where to look… In a way, I think I experienced some of that same fever the “professional” tomb raiders talked about.

    According to recent reports, RV: The Witch’s Mouth is an ensemble novel with a lot of different characters, but it revolves around Bardo. He’s almost a godfather-type figure in the way he involves so many different kinds of people in his activities and spreads the wealth he earns. Tell us about your inspiration for creating him.

    SN: Everything that happens in the novel is inspired by the interviews I mentioned earlier. But the characters are entirely the product of my imagination, as are the main plot and the various subplots.

    According to recent reports, when it comes to Bardo, I did a little “plundering” myself. Based on the stories I heard, I imagined this guy who, even as a kid, recognized the value of these artifacts, which everyone else treated like useless old junk taking up space.

    It has been revealed that but Bardo is also a man of action, and a pretty clever one. He knows how hard life is for the families of Populonia. He starts getting them to hand over their “pieces,” as they call them in the trade, and then sells them to the more experienced tomb raiders in the Tuscia region, returning with the money. Real money, not a few pennies.

    Industry observers note that before long, everyone starts looking at Bardo like a sort of saint. Everyone is knocking on his door with an artifact in their hand. And Bardo is extremely good at weaving a network built on trust and gratitude. That means protection—Bardo is untouchable. This is something else that fascinated me: at least in the beginning, there wasn’t a gun in sight. But then the operation grows exponentially. Billions of lire start pouring in. And where there’s that much money, guns usually follow.

    According to recent reports, RV: Of the novel’s many great characters, I was fascinated by Elisa, Bardo’s wife; Silvana, the prostitute; and the Marquis. As you write, do you have favorites? Do some of the characters come more easily to you than others?

    SN: Obviously I love them all, not only because of the role they each play in the story—a character is always an opportunity to explore different points of view, different lives and legacies… What I mean is, how does a particular character, with their own history, react to certain events? That’s part of the magic of writing. Especially when we explore uncomfortable aspects of human nature and relationships.

    Industry observers note that that remarked, among the characters you mentioned, Silvana and the Marchese have a special place in my heart. Silvana truly is the queen (I should say, the Principessa) of the novel. The Marchese, for his part, embodies a desperation that is part of the landscape and is compounded by his broken dreams, a desperation that still moves me. Although in the end… but I’d better stop here.

    RV: In many ways, this is the story of a gang of tomb robbers but it’s also the story of an ecosystem of stolen goods and people.

    Sources indicate that SN: I had some interesting experiences in this respect during the promotion of the book in Italy. Together with my Italian publishers, we had the wonderful idea of organizing some events in archaeological museums. Some of the events were fantastic. In other cases, though, for instance in Vetulonia, the director of the magnificent local museum declined to participate. He didn’t want to celebrate, right in a place designed to house Etruscan artifacts, a story about thieves who had deprived everyone of the opportunity to admire works of art and experience the sense of connection we can feel with the people who lived in distant times.

    But I’m not an educator; I’m a novelist. I try to make sense of the world through stories. Even if these stories are unsettling—in fact, all the better. What I’m saying is, “Hey, look, this happened too.” I’m saying, “Hey, look at how these people lived. How they reacted, what they dreamt about, what circumstances led them to make certain choices.” And I know very well that it’s wrong to prevent the public from viewing a work of art, locking it away instead in some billionaire’s safe.

    Industry observers note that I’ll go further. For me, the real damage inflicted by tomb raiders is not the sale of a particular artifact to a private collector. The real theft—and maybe it’s the novelist in me talking—has to do with removing a clue (the artifact itself) from the place where it was found, thereby interrupting a story. Otherwise, archaeologists would be able to tell us how people loved, what clothes they wore or what food they ate, what gods they worshipped, what stories they passed down in that very place. This is what they rob us of, to make a few million dollars. I hope that somehow, between the lines of my novel, this message comes across. But according to some museum directors, I’ve missed the mark.

    RV: Are there other novels or writers you draw inspiration from in your work?

    Industry observers note that SN: The list would be endless, stretching from my formative years to the present, now that I’ve just turned fifty. It would comprise all the different kinds of writing I’ve sought out, explored, and measured myself against. And yet I feel like I’m just starting out.

    According to recent reports, to mention some writers that have a place in my heart, in no particular order: Italo Calvino, Stephen King, Albert Camus, Joyce Carol Oates, John Steinbeck, Chuck Palahniuk, Beppe Fenoglio, Ágota Kristóf, Mikhail Bulgakov. If you asked me again a minute from now, the list would be completely different. I’m thinking of John Fante, or the fantasy novels I adored as a teenager. And what about Dumas and his Count of Monte Cristo?

    Seriously, I never know how to answer this question. But I think that each of these writers has given me a great gift: they “gave me permission” to be brave. To let my imagination spill onto the page, for what it’s worth. And all the voices that come with it.

    RV: What are you reading and/or working on at the moment?

    Industry observers note that SN: On my nightstand are books by David Szalay and Ernest Jünger—the latter a special gift I received, a book that I’ve already read but want to reread. Recently, I returned to John Fante’s Wait Until Spring, Bandini after many years—what a knockout. I don’t think it will ever get old. I also really loved Tiffany McDaniel’s The Summer That Melted Everything.

    On my computer is a novel forthcoming in Italy, Il ronzio (“The Buzzing”), which is in the final stages of editing. Of course, I’m also working on another novel. And I’m having fun writing the treatment for a TV series, which is due soon. And listen to this: after twenty years of writing books, for the first time ever, there’s a police inspector in one of my stories. I never would have imagined it.

    Radha Vatsal is the Film/TV Columnist for CrimeReads. She is the author of No. 10 Doyers Street and the Kitty Weeks mysteries, and her essays have appeared in the The New York Times, The Atlantic, the Los Angeles Review of Books, and elsewhere. She holds a Ph.D. in Film History from Duke University. You can find her on Instagram or email: rvatsal@lithub.com.

    #8908. Medieval Settings Are Back In These Mysteries, Thrillers, and Horror Novels

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1393 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Medieval Settings Are Back In These Mysteries, Thrillers, and Horror Novels

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There’s a whole new wave of excellent new genre fiction set in medieval Europe, and since my mother was a medievalist, and I love to mention that fact, I figured I’d do a quick roundup of some new and upcoming releases.
    • Note: This list is organized in chronological order of setting.
    • Anderson, Nicked (Pantheon Books) Setting: Mediterranean Medieval World, 11th Century.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There’s a whole new wave of excellent new genre fiction set in medieval Europe, and since my mother was a medievalist, and I love to mention that fact, I figured I’d do a quick roundup of some new and upcoming releases. Before I get to the recommendations, you may be wondering: what time period exactly are we talking? For the purposes of this article, the medieval era is roughly defined as between 1000-1500, depending on where the characters live. For example: 15th century Italy = Renaissance. 15th century Estonia = Medieval. Burgundy, I suppose, is half and half. Periodization is a continuum much more than a series of hard stops and new beginnings, and the Renaissance is just the Middle Ages with better marketing (see Inventing the Renaissance for more on the debate).

    Note: This list is organized in chronological order of setting. Most are upcoming releases from this year or next year, but there are two older titles that are still recent enough to count for this trend. Books that are not yet published have their publication dates next to their publisher info. If you’ve got any Dark Ages-set mysteries to recommend to me, please comment, because I would very much like to read them.

    M. T. Anderson, Nicked (Pantheon Books) Setting: Mediterranean Medieval World, 11th Century.

    This came out in 2024, which I consider recent enough to include as part of this trend piece—especially when considering a medieval time scale. Also it’s awesome. In Nicked, a group of disparate travelers sets off on an odyssey of the medieval world with a common 11th century mission: they’ve been hired to steal the Anatolian relics of a powerful saint and transport them to an Italian city state in hopes of sparking more commerce from pilgrims (the medieval equivalent of taking the Dodgers from Brooklyn to LA). Along the way, they form deep bonds, some blossoming into romance, and take in the sights and sounds of the entire Mediterranean world. M. T. Anderson does that rare feat of capturing the spirit of the time, granting readers a lively, Rabelaisian interpretation of an unfairly maligned era (see history book The Bright Ages for further appreciation).

    Paul Brous, The Undying Lamb (Rising Action) Setting: Italian states, 1230.

    Industry observers note that when a book starts with a glossary featuring words from several now-dead languages, you just know that it’s going to be impeccably researched. In Paul Brous’ medieval-set thriller, an Albigensian assassin and an English knight must protect a child with an inconvenient lineage, as a vast array of forces attempt to eliminate their vulnerable charge. Perfect for those who enjoyed Conclave, but wish it had been set waaaay further back in history.

    James Bennett, Mother of Night (Evil Twin, March 2027) Setting: Holy Roman Empire, 1291.

    In this intense work of historical horror, Saladin’s victories have sent a ragged group of crusaders fleeing from the Holy Land, their only option to board a rickety vessel soon enough broken by stormy seas. Shipwrecked and far from home, the few survivors find succor and strangeness amongst a group of miserable swamp-dwellers who warn of danger ahead; the crusaders, determined to forge ahead, do not listen, with predictably dire consequences and a surprising amount of singing.

    Ferdia Lennon, Brother Nothing (Holt, June 2027) Setting: France, 1369.

    According to recent reports, set just a decade before the events of Doom Painting, Brother Nothing follows a newly appointed provost and his precociously intelligent daughter as they flee plague-ridden Paris for a town in the North of France. While their new abode does appear safe from pestilence, other dangers are many, including the perennial threat of English soldiers, an epidemic of children gone missing, and a murder pinned on a prodigal son who confesses to every possible crime— save the crime of which he is accused. As the provost uncovers layer after layer of shocking crimes and terrifying cover-ups, he and his few allies begin to suspect the entire town of conspiracy, for what reads a bit like Red Harvest, medieval style.

    Industry observers note that A.K. Blakemore, Doom Painting (Scribner, April 2027) Setting: England, 1381.

    Sources indicate that I have complete trust in A.K. Blakemore’s power to render historical fiction as vivid and complex as depictions of the present, and her new novel of the English Peasant’s Revolt does not disappoint. In 1381, England’s most oppressed rose up against the conditions of their serfdom, driven to rebellion by the devastation of the plague and the endless war with France. For 16 days, they challenged the notion that some should rule while others serve, embodied by Wat Tyler’s epic call-to-arms: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then a gentleman?” As a side note, I’ve been planning to get a tattoo of that slogan in Ye Olde Englishe font for a while now, so maybe it’s time to bite the bullet. Also the book confirms what I have always known: Wat Tyler had major sex appeal.

    Indrek Hargla, The Secret of Saint Olaf’s Church Translated by Adam Cullen (Pushkin Press) Setting: 15th Century Tallinn.

    Indrek Hargla’s tale of a crime-solving apothecary is based in obscure, and very real, history; the mystery unraveled by the amateur sleuth takes its jumping off point from a mysterious note in Latvian historical records, for a richly detailed and vividly imagined take on a high-water mark in Latvia’s regional influence. In The Secret of Saint Olaf’s Church, the murder of an aging knight leads a city luminary towards a horrifying secret with deep implications for the city’s fragile economic status and unstable power structure.

    Indrek Hargla, The Ghost of Rataskaevu Street (Pushkin Press) Setting: Estonia, 1419.

    Recent findings suggest that hargla’s second novel to feature apothecary Melchior, released for the first time in the US this month, takes his hero on a dark journey stretching far into the city’s past. When three different townspeople die just after seeing a ghost, the pharmacist and amateur sleuth decides to dig into the matter. In between brewing tinctures, infusing remedies, and proscribing his usual treatments, Melchior keeps circling back to a house in the center of town, once the setting of a terrible crime, and key to understanding the more recent killings.

    Jo Harkin, The Pretender Setting: England, Ireland, Burgundy, 15th Century.

    Sources indicate that at the tail end of the Wars of the Roses, an ordinary farm boy is plucked from his simple village life and trained up to become a king. He’s been swapped for a commoner at birth by his dead Earl of a father and forgotten about in the midst of internecine warfare; now, he’s the last hope for the house of York to triumph over its Tudor rivals. But does he have the stuff it takes to fight through his own doubts and become king? And will he survive the endless sacrifices demanded in his ascent to the throne? This is an excellent book to help you understand the inspirations behind Game of Thrones, or the power politics of Elaine’s kingdom in Wheel of Time.

    Katherine Arden, The Unicorn Hunter (Del Rey) Setting: Brittany, Late 15th Century.

    In 15th century Brittany, a noblewoman facing an unwanted union with a far-away lord puts in motion a clever proposal to hold off the wedding: her husband-to-be must join her in a unicorn hunt in the dense, dark forest near to her castle. Soon, they find themselves transported into a magical realm beset by an ancient curse that only the lady and her wooing courtiers can break. The Unicorn Hunter takes its inspiration from the real Anne of Brittany, whose marriage to the King of France was just another method of preserving what little sovereignty her province could hold onto under the steady creep of French imperial influence, and who brought two beds to her wedding as a symbol of her independence. I think I would have quite liked Anne of Brittany—Katharine Arden certainly feels a sprightly kinship with the impish aristocrat.

    Molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (380 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As longtime CrimeReads readers (“CrimeReaders”) know, the editors of this website are always interested in news related to the Loch Ness Monster.
    • Any Loch Ness Monster-related news intrigues me.
    • It’s set near Loch Ness, obviously, and it’s about a young, irascible, beautiful London detective who winds up being kicked out (I think?) of her job, only to wind up investigating a personal matter near Inverness… and being drawn into a strange mystery near Loch Ness.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As longtime CrimeReads readers (“CrimeReaders”) know, the editors of this website are always interested in news related to the Loch Ness Monster. Especially me. For example, several years ago, I wrote about how, in 2016, a bunch of Norwegian scientists had sent a high-tech robot down into Loch Ness to scan the, and the robot sent back sonar scans of a creature that looked exactly like the Loch Ness monster, but actually, it turned out to be a model of the Loch Ness Monster built for the 1969 film The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes that had accidentally sunk during filming. So that was a bummer. A HILARIOUS bummer, but a bummer nonetheless.

    Any Loch Ness Monster-related news intrigues me. So you can imagine my delight when I came across news of an upcoming series from the BBC and BritBox. It’s called The Loch Ness Mysteries.

    It’s set near Loch Ness, obviously, and it’s about a young, irascible, beautiful London detective who winds up being kicked out (I think?) of her job, only to wind up investigating a personal matter near Inverness… and being drawn into a strange mystery near Loch Ness.

    So, in the words of the genius who wrote the BBC’s press release, “from Scotland Yard to Scotland Scotland.”.

    According to recent reports, also, what’s the beautiful, brilliant, difficult detective’s name? DCI Vanessa “Nessie” Keen.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas answers questions during a visit to the University of Texas at Austin on April 15, 2026. (Photo by Eric Gay/The Associated Press).

    In a recent development, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas will lead an undergraduate seminar at the University of Texas at Austin on race, equality and political thought in February.

    The one-credit-hour seminar, “CIV 166 Equality and the Latest Birth of Freedom,” will include two hours of lecture daily from Feb. 1 to Feb. 5, 2027, for 17 students. Sixty-five applied.

    Students will also meet with Justin Dyer, the dean of the University of Texas at Austin’s School of Civic Leadership, during the seminar, which follows American political thought from the nation’s founding through the Civil War to the present.

    According to recent reports, readings include the writings and speeches of Frederick Douglass, Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois, as well as civil rights leaders the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X. The course examines how questions of race and equality show up in recent Supreme Court decisions.

    Thomas previously spoke to students and legal professionals at the University of Texas at Austin in April, making the case that the Supreme Court’s failures have stemmed from a lack of courage, not a lack of understanding, and he discussed Plessy v. Ferguson, a 1896 ruling that upheld government-enforced segregation.

    Thomas, who joined the Supreme Court in 1991, is its longest-serving current member.

    #8901. 8 nonfiction books that delve into the darkest parts of sports

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1433 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    8 nonfiction books that delve into the darkest parts of sports

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1433 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’d given up smoking and the weight I was steadily gaining was regularly making me cry.
    • Industry observers note that in reality, it took me thirteen years and two nervous breakdowns before I finally ran a mile in 7:57, not long after I ran off (not literally) with a vicar.
    • Here are eight books that each reveal a particularly dark but also compelling vision of hot sporting hell.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I took up running in 2010. I’d given up smoking and the weight I was steadily gaining was regularly making me cry. My partner at the time had been a serious competitive runner and believed I’d be able to just knock out an eight-minute mile.

    Industry observers note that in reality, it took me thirteen years and two nervous breakdowns before I finally ran a mile in 7:57, not long after I ran off (not literally) with a vicar. Somewhere in the middle of all that, I’d managed to reach number six in the UK for over-forties women’s tennis. It has gradually dawned on me that sporting success isn’t the healthy, glossy, happybodymaxx endeavour that shiny people on Instagram would have us all believe.

    Here are eight books that each reveal a particularly dark but also compelling vision of hot sporting hell.

    Andre Agassi, Open: An Autobiography.

    I read Open when I was on the verge of my own tennis-related nervous breakdown (alas not involving crystal meth like Agassi’s), during a heatwave in Nottingham, in a hotel room full of little flies that I’d become convinced were going to bite me and cause such a severe allergic reaction that I would die. The prologue is one of the best pieces of writing I’ve ever encountered: the extraordinary violence of a five-set tennis match, ending with the wounded competitors lying side by side, holding hands.

    Recent findings suggest that then there’s Agassi’s father’s $10,000 bet (later reduced to $500) that his nine-year-old son could beat Jim Brown, the famous American Football player. The fact that the book was ghostwritten (by the wonderful J. R. Moehringer) gives it an additional layer of weirdness and gothic edge for me.

    Rafael Nadal (with John Carlin), Rafa.

    This is basically an OCD-fest (although officially Nadal does not have this condition) about Rafa being bullied to sporting success by his Uncle Toni. There’s a chilling story about Toni refusing to let seven-year-old Rafa have a replacement bottle of water to teach him a lesson about losing the first one (you don’t need a psychotherapist to make the link with the water bottle shenanigans on court), and another about telling him he must never make himself the center of attention, even when he was the best tennis player in the world.

    Industry observers note that even as an adult, Nadal describes extraordinary anxieties, including the belief that if he makes a small mistake, his mother might die. The contrast between the superhuman control Nadal displays on the tennis court and the terrifying lack of control he feels everywhere else is what makes this such a disturbing and compelling memoir.

    Serena Williams (with Daniel Paisner), My Life: Queen of the Court.

    There’s a brilliant scene in the incredible Teddy Perkins episode of Atlanta where Teddy, played by Donald Glover, does a roll-call of famous fathers who have abused their children towards greatness. He mentions Joe Jackson, Tiger Woods’s father and Richard Williams.

    Like Andre Agassi’s father, Richard Williams was seemingly determined to create a tennis champion, trying the sport with his older daughters before it finally stuck with his youngest two, Venus and Serena. He would take them to the local tennis courts in Compton with shopping trolleys full of tennis balls. Initially, Venus was the more successful and Serena was determined to beat her own sister so she did not simply become a footnote in Venus’s story.

    Leanne Shapton, Swimming Studies.

    According to recent reports, swimming Studies was actually the book that set me off on my disastrous tennis adventure. It was a single line in it, something about how Leanne Shapton, recovered from her dark sporting childhood, was still placing in “age-group” events. It was those two words, age-group, that made me think perhaps I could resurrect my childhood tennis dreams.

    When I read Swimming Studies, I was myself trying to swim seriously, but ended up with breaststroker’s knee—which is odd, as Shapton suffered exactly the same thing. I felt a little like the book was haunting me, and that I was literally absorbing its ailments quasi-gothically.

    Brad Gilbert (with Steve Jamison), Winning Ugly.

    According to recent reports, this was basically my bible during the year I played competitive tennis. Actually, that’s wrong. The Inner Game of Tennis was my bible. This was my grimoire. This may be one of the most fun dark books ever written.

    Industry observers note that basically, Brad Gilbert tells you how you can win at tennis (and maybe even life too)—even if you are shit. You do things like turn up early and have a hit on the court with a local coach (impossible when I tried it), then shower, change and arrive late for the match and suggest starting with no warm up. Gilbert has lots of handy hints for ways to deliberately psych out your opponents with chat specifically designed to derail them.

    Adharanand Finn, The Way of the Runner.

    I really loved Finn’s previous book, Running with the Kenyans, which begins with a stirring account of him unexpectedly winning a 5K fun run. After that he goes to Kenya, meets some Massive Characters who introduce themselves with their marathon PBs, and becomes himself a more excellent runner. It’s uplifting and inspiring.

    Industry observers note that but this book about Japanese running methods is far darker. Finn begins this one battling injury and exhaustion and then encounters the weird, workaholic training methods of the Japanese, including running with exaggeratedly short strides and accelerated cadence. There was something bleakly joyless about this book compared with the first one, but I still hoovered it up.

    Christopher McDougall, Born to Run.

    Reading Born to Run isn’t like reading a normal book—it’s an era of your life. My heart skips and I get goosebumps just thinking about it. The ecstatic descriptions of people for whom running is both a way of life and a form of transport, and the theories about primal living, squatting and running barefoot, would go on to underpin my philosophy of sport and life for years to come (and still do).

    After reading this book I became a primal forefoot runner. My friend Vybarr Cregan-Reid, author of Footnotes: How Running Makes Us Human, went totally barefoot, despite various broken-glass incidents in British parks. I will never forget the wonderfully compelling romance of Jenn Shelton and Billy “Bonehead” Barnett, and how they would eat pizza and drink Mountain Dew in the middle of their ultras, like running was something even Lana Del Rey could do.

    Oh, how I loved this dark and crazy book that made running seem like part religion and part disco-party where everyone successfully hides their pain.

    W. Timothy Gallwey, The Inner Game of Tennis.

    The Inner Game of Tennis changed my entire life and philosophy, and there’s nothing darker than that. I found myself using it as a way of understanding EVERYTHING. The concept is that you have two selves. Self 1 and Self 2. Self 2 will quietly do things if you just leave it alone, but Self 1 is constantly judging. During my disastrous tennis adventure, I could never really get rid of Self 1 and its constant voicings of my coming glory, imminent failure, place in the rankings, what I’d tell my coach, etc.

    According to recent reports, one of the tricks Gallwey recommends is reading the writing on the tennis ball as it comes towards you. I’ve encountered this kind of method in other places too, like reciting your own phone number backwards during a panic attack.

    It has been revealed that another dark sports book I still live by is Steve Peters’s The Chimp Paradox, which has some similar ideas about quieting the crazed ego-animal within. Ultimately, if you can let Self 2 take control, you can enter the mythic space of the Zone or Flow, which is, according to Daniel Kahneman’s incredible book Thinking, Fast and Slow, the most optimal place a human can reach.

    It has been revealed that scarlett Thomas was born in London. She is the author of highly acclaimed contemporary cult novels including The End of Mr. Y, which was longlisted for the Orange Broadband Prize for Fiction; Oligarchy; The Seed Collectors; PopCo; The Sleepwalkers; The Runner; and the Worldquake series of middle grade books. Her novels have sold over half a million copies worldwide and been translated into twenty-six languages. Scarlett is professor of creative writing and contemporary fiction at the University of Kent. Find out more at ScarThomas.com.

    #8900. Latest Update: Andrey Zvyagintsev on Marriage, Mythology, and the Violence of Family Life

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1743 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Andrey Zvyagintsev on Marriage, Mythology, and the Violence of Family Life

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the emotional punch in the gut of Andrey Zvyagintsev’s debut feature, The Return (2003), about an estranged father who takes his two teenage sons on a camping trip, has remained with me, even though I first saw it more than twenty years ago at the Toronto Film Festival.
